C5 (no CWE): the sentinel loop at line 191 depends on seccomp_x86_64_extra_arches/seccomp_aarch64_extra_arches being 0-terminated; both arrays are defined outside the fragment, and their content is static framework data, not attacker input, so neither non-termination nor overrun is provable here.

C6 (no CWE): the temp file is created in the fixed directory "/tmp" at line 263, but filename generation/entropy lives inside glnx_open_anonymous_tmpfile_full (not shown), so CWE-377 is not confirmable from the fragment.

C7 (no CWE): allowed_personality (gulong) is passed to SCMP_A0(SCMP_CMP_NE, ...) at line 124; any narrowing or truncation to the syscall word width occurs inside libseccomp and is not visible in the fragment.
The condition `if (r < 0 && r == -EFAULT)` at lines 217/235 is a redundant conjunction, but its only security consequence is subsumed by limitation C1.

verdict.summary: digest_generic_verify feeds the unchecked signed result of digest_length(d) into xmalloc and crypto_memneq. With no visible constraint on len, a negative value is implicitly widened to a huge size_t at both call sites, corrupting the allocation size and the comparison length and leading to allocation failure with continued use of the pointer, or an oversized allocation/comparison (crash/DoS).

evidence.reason: Allocation-size sink: len originates at line 4 from digest_length(d) and no shown statement constrains it, leaving the full int domain; a negative value (e.g., -1) is implicitly converted to a huge size_t (SIZE_MAX) at this call site, so the size argument is out of the domain an allocation requires, and the corrupted value is consumed as a security-relevant allocation size (primary CWE-195 mechanism).

Length sink: the same int len from line 4 reaches the length argument with no check on the path (line 10 guards only digest_final's status and executes after the allocation). For negative len the int-to-size_t widening makes the requested comparison length huge, so the length argument is not provably in-domain; md's capacity is not visible and tmp's capacity equals the same corrupted size, so the confirmed mechanism is the signed-to-unsigned length/size conversion (CWE-195), not a provably excess read.

assumptions: xmalloc and crypto_memneq take size_t size/length arguments (standard name-implied semantics used for the call-site domain analysis).
digest_length's return is assigned to int, so its residual domain in this fragment is the full int range; no statement in the fragment establishes a non-negative bound.
limitations: Whether digest_length can actually return a negative value in the full program is not shown here; the finding rests on the residual-range rule (no visible constraint) rather than a demonstrated producer, hence the capped confidence.

A NULL-dereference chain (xmalloc failure returning NULL, then digest_final(d, tmp) at line 9) depends on unshown xmalloc failure semantics and on digest_final's unshown body; not independently confirmed.
An out-of-bounds read of md by crypto_memneq is not demonstrable because md's backing capacity is not declared in the fragment.
A NULL md would be caller-supplied with no producer in the shown code; out of scope.
If an external contract guarantees digest_length returns a non-negative value, the trigger is impossible; that invariant is not visible in the fragment and cannot support a safe verdict.

verdict.summary: xml_parse_node recurses on attacker-controlled input with no depth limit in the shown code: per element nesting (line 83) and per PI/comment (lines 24, 40). A document of N nested elements (e.g., '<a>' repeated N times) is admitted by every shown guard and drives recursion depth N, exhausting the finite process stack and crashing the parser (uncontrolled recursion, DoS).

evidence.reason: Entry-point scanner content (attacker-controlled; only positionally constrained: line 8 requires '<', lines 12/28 require next byte not '?';'!', lines 80-81 admit '<' followed by any non-'/' non-'!' byte) drives an unbounded nesting recursion. Witness ''*N+''*N passes line 8, skips 12/28, passes 53 ('>' terminator), 68 (not '/'), 76, and 80-81 ('a' after '<') at every level, so each level re-enters this sink at line 83; the fragment contains no depth cap or limit statement, so depth equals N and exhausts the stack (primary CWE-674, uncontrolled recursion; attacker-triggerable DoS).

Same uncontrolled-recursion flaw via processing instructions: input such as N consecutive '<?x?>' constructs is admitted by lines 8 and 12 ('<?' pair), the terminating loop at 14-23 completes on each '?>', and each occurrence of this sink adds one stack frame with no depth bound in the shown code, contributing to stack exhaustion (CWE-674).

Same uncontrolled-recursion flaw via comments: input of N consecutive '<!--x-->' constructs is admitted by line 8 and line 28 ('<!'), the loop at 30-39 completes on each '>', and each occurrence of this sink adds one unguarded stack frame with no depth limit visible in the fragment (CWE-674).

assumptions: scanner carries attacker-supplied XML bytes and is treated as entry-point input because the shown code is a pull parser that directly consumes *scanner->curptr.

L109 'if (get_char != '<' || get_char != '/')' is read as two sequential reads with || short-circuit: it requires '<' then '/', i.e., the intended '</' token; only the error path skips the second read.
on_syntax_error is assumed not to return; the fragment never checks its outcome, so the parser's behavior if it did return is out of scope for verdicts.
PJ_CHECK_STACK() at line 6 is a compile option stack-usage check, not a recursion-depth or input-bound check, so it does not cap the recursion analyzed here.
limitations: PI, comment, and CDATA loops (lines 14-23, 30-39, 98-103) contain no EOF exit; for attacker inputs without '?>', '>', or ']]>' respectively, termination is not established by the shown code. Whether that manifests as a hang (CWE-835) or out-of-bounds read depends on the unshown pj_scan_get_until_ch / pj_scan_advance_n EOF semantics and the unshown scanner buffer capacity, so it is demoted, not a confirmed finding.

Reads of *scanner->curptr and *(scanner->curptr+1) (lines 8, 12, 17, 45, 53, 67, 68, 70, 76, 80-81, 88, 93, 109) could be out of bounds at stream end, but the scanner buffer capacity/end and any EOF sentinel are not identifiable from the fragment, so OOB (CWE-125) is unconfirmable.

attr->value.slen -= 2 (line 62) after pj_scan_get_quotes (line 59) could underflow if the quote scan yields slen < 2, but pj_scan_get_quotes' minimum-length contract and pj_str_t.slen signedness are not shown, and no in-fragment consumer uses the value; no finding.

NULL dereference via unchecked alloc_node/alloc_attr results (lines 44-50, 54-56) is not confirmable because the helpers' failure contract is not visible; allocation failure is not a shown path to NULL.
Potential OOB/underrun of any token (name, attributes, content, end_name) is likewise unconfirmable: capacities derive from unshown helpers, and no in-fragment memory write uses these lengths.

The always-advancing for(;;) loops make at least one byte of progress per iteration inside the buffer, so a definite non-termination verdict would also require demonstrated EOF behavior (see first limitation).

verdict.summary: ReadPCLImage writes formatted output into heap buffers density/options that are allocated as copies of "" (1 byte) at lines 186-187, passing MagickPathExtent as the length to FormatLocaleString. The minimum rendered output ("0x0\0", 4 bytes; "-g0x0 \0", 8 bytes) already exceeds capacity for every admitted input, so attacker-controlled PCL content (MediaBox geometry, resolution) triggers a heap-based buffer overflow (CWE-122) on every parse path past the delegate lookup.

evidence.reason: density is allocated at line 186 as density=AcquireString(""); by the name-implied copy semantics applied to the visible empty-string argument, the heap object has capacity 1 byte. FormatLocaleString is a standard format-into-buffer call whose destination capacity is the caller's object; the shown code passes declared length MagickPathExtent (capacity of the fixed arrays at lines 9/11/12/14), not the real 1-byte capacity. Byte account: %g of 0.0 yields "0x0" = 4 bytes and of 72.0 yields "72x72" = 6 bytes (each + NUL), so every admitted resolution (unconstrained between lines 83-96 and this sink) writes >= 3 bytes past the end of the 1-byte allocation (CWE-122 heap-based buffer overflow). Guards on the path (OpenBlob status line 65, AcquireUniqueSymbolicLink line 71, delegate_info non-NULL line 177) all admit an ordinary openable PCL file.

options is allocated at line 187 as options=AcquireString(""); capacity 1 byte. page.width/page.height derive entirely inside the shown code from attacker file bytes: MediaBox [0 0 612 792] parses via sscanf (line 142, count==4 admitted by line 148), width=(size_t)floor(bounds.x2-bounds.x1+0.5) (line 153), page.width=width (line 156). For that witness FormatLocaleString writes "-g612x792 \0" = 11 bytes into the 1-byte allocation -> heap OOB write of 10 bytes (CWE-122); even a zero-size page renders "-g0x0 " = 8 bytes, so every admitted page geometry overflows.

Same 1-byte density allocation (line 186): when image_info->ping is not MagickFalse (entry-point input field, no shown constraint), the literal "2.0x2.0" renders 7 chars + NUL = 8 bytes into the 1-byte density object, an additional heap OOB write of 7 bytes on the same sink path as the primary finding (CWE-122).

assumptions: MagickPathExtent >= 2: the fragment itself uses MagickPathExtent as the size of filename/command buffers that must hold paths (e.g., CopyMagickString into filename at line 212), so the passed length is at least 2; the overflow occurs for any MagickPathExtent >= 2.

AcquireString is treated by its name-implied contract as returning an exact heap copy of its argument; a copy of the visible argument "" (lines 186-187) has capacity 1 byte. No shown statement assigns a larger capacity, reallocates, or resizes these objects before the sinks.

Reachability of lines 186-195 requires GetDelegateInfo to return non-NULL (guard at line 177); in the fragment's straight-line flow this is the deployment condition for a configured PCL delegate, satisfied on standard ImageMagick installs.
limitations: Command-accumulation loop (lines 108-159) is bounded: the guard at lines 116-117 admits continuing only while p-command <= MagickPathExtent-2 after the post-increment, so the data write at line 115 reaches at most index MagickPathExtent-2 and the NUL at line 119 at most index MagickPathExtent-1, both within command[MagickPathExtent] declared at line 9; no OOB.

Delegate command construction (lines 214-218) and execution (lines 221-222): the format template from GetDelegateCommands(delegate_info) is not visible, and the concrete arguments are numeric or unique-generated names, so command/argument injection is not confirmable from the fragment.

ExternalDelegateCommand status is discarded (line 221), but the subsequent ReadImage NULL check at line 227 catches delegate failure, so no security-relevant operation demonstrably runs on the failure state.

count is not reset per loop iteration (lines 101-159), so a successful MediaBox parse persists into later non-matching commands and reuses stale bounds; the stale doubles only affect numeric page geometry values with no security-relevant consumer.

double-to-size_t conversions of extreme MediaBox doubles (lines 153-154, 192-193) are UB for out-of-range values, but the converted values are consumed only by %g formatting into the sinks above; no index/size/capacity/pointer-arithmetic consumer, so no independent integer-overflow finding.

Unchecked AcquireString/CloneImageInfo results (lines 186-187, 197) were not reported: allocation-failure NULL dereference requires an unchecked-allocation failure with no security-relevant operation on the failure state shown; AcquireString is fatal-abort by contract.

Additional same-mechanism FormatLocaleString writes into the 1-byte options buffer at lines 202-203 and 205-207 (when read_info->number_scenes != 0) exist but are not separately evidenced; line 194 already overflows unconditionally before them.
geometry (line 168) is formatted but never used afterward; no sink.

The double rendered by %g is never negative/infinite in a way that changes the write-length conclusion: the minimum admitted render ("0x0") already exceeds the 1-byte capacity, so the finding does not depend on boundary values.

verdict.summary: The seccomp rule-add status checks at lines 218 and 236 only treat r == -EFAULT (identified by the code's own comment as the benign 'unknown syscall' case) as an error. Any other negative return from seccomp_rule_add (e.g., -ENOMEM/-EINVAL, meaning the block rule was not installed) is silently discarded, the policy-building loops continue, and setup_seccomp returns TRUE at line 275 with the sandbox's syscall blocklist incomplete; because line 147 selects SCMP_ACT_ALLOW as the default action, the unblocked syscall remains allowed in the filter exported at line 267 and delivered to bubblewrap at lines 272-273. This inverts fail-open/fail-closed behavior: a genuine rule-install failure is ignored while the benign unknown-syscall case aborts setup.

evidence.snippet:
if (r < 0 && r == -EFAULT /* unknown syscall */)
        return flatpak_fail_error (error, FLATPAK_ERROR_SETUP_FAILED, _("Failed to block syscall %d"), scall);
evidence.reason: r is the int return of seccomp_rule_add (lines 215/217); its residual range is the full API return domain (0 on success, negative errno on failure) with no shown constraint before this guard. The guard's admitted fatal set is exactly {r == -EFAULT}, which the code's own comment identifies as the benign 'unknown syscall' case, while every real failure outcome (r < 0, r != -EFAULT, e.g. -ENOMEM/-EINVAL) falls through the loop and reaches return TRUE at line 275. Since line 147 installed SCMP_ACT_ALLOW as the default action, the syscall whose rule failed to install stays allowed in the filter exported at 267 and delivered at 272-273 — the sandbox blocklist is silently incomplete while setup reports success (CWE-754, improper handling of the rule-add return status; fail-open on genuine failures, fail-closed on the benign case).

evidence.snippet:
if (r < 0 && r == -EFAULT /* unknown syscall */)
            return flatpak_fail_error (error, FLATPAK_ERROR_SETUP_FAILED, _("Failed to block syscall %d"), scall);
evidence.reason: Same inverted status check for the non-devel blocklist: r from seccomp_rule_add (lines 231/234) is treated as fatal only for r == -EFAULT ('unknown syscall' per the inline comment); all other negative returns (rule-install failures such as -ENOMEM/-EINVAL) are discarded, the loop at 224 continues, and setup_seccomp returns TRUE at 275 with the personality/ptrace/perf_event_open block rules potentially absent while SCMP_ACT_ALLOW (line 147) leaves those syscalls permitted (CWE-754).

assumptions: G_N_ELEMENTS (lines 207, 224, 245) evaluates to the exact element counts of the static arrays declared in the fragment (syscall_blocklist lines 45-112, syscall_nondevel_blocklist lines 114-127, socket_family_allowlist lines 129-142), so strict-inequality loop bounds keep all table accesses in-bounds.
seccomp_rule_add returns 0 on success and a negative errno when it does not install a rule; the fragment's own use of r as a status at lines 215-218 and 231-236 relies on this contract.
The default seccomp action SCMP_ACT_ALLOW (line 147) means any syscall without a successfully installed block rule remains allowed in the emitted filter.
glnx_open_anonymous_tmpfile_full at line 264 creates an anonymous seekable regular tmpfile, so lseek at line 270 operates on a seekable fd.
limitations: extra_arches sentinel loop (line 192): seccomp_x86_64_extra_arches / seccomp_aarch64_extra_arches (lines 163, 173) are not defined in the fragment, so the 0-sentinel termination and array capacity are unconfirmable; the arrays are not attacker-influenced in any case.

arch (line 2): the fragment imposes no length or NUL-termination constraint; a non-terminated string would overrun inside strcmp (lines 156-170), but the buffer capacity is not identifiable from the shown code, so the OOB claim is unconfirmable.
Discarded returns of lseek (line 270) and flatpak_bwrap_add_args_data_fd (lines 272-273) have no demonstrable security-relevant failure state within the fragment.
seccomp_rule_add_exact failures (lines 257, 262) are deliberately ignored per the fragment's own comment at lines 241-243; treated as documented behavior, not a finding.
The r == -EFAULT branch (lines 218-219, 236-237) also aborts sandbox setup when a syscall is unknown to libseccomp — an availability facet of the same inverted condition, not an independent finding.

Exploiting the fail-open path requires the libseccomp library to return a non-EFAULT negative errno (e.g., -ENOMEM), which the fragment's own data cannot force; attacker control of that failure is not demonstrated.

verdict.summary: ComputeAsync computes n = input.dim_size(ndims - 1) and nrhs = rhs.dim_size(ndims - 1) at lines 5-6 before the rank checks at lines 9 and 12. A rank-0 input makes ndims - 1 == -1, and a right-hand side with rank less than the input rank makes ndims - 1 >= rhs.dims(); both call TensorShape::dim_size with an out-of-domain index, producing an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) that can crash the process or leak memory.

evidence.reason: dim_size's parameter is consumed as a dimension index with valid domain [0, input.dims()); ndims = input.dims() (line 4) is entry-point-controlled and unconstrained before this call because the only rank guard, ndims >= 2, executes later (lines 8-11). Witness: rank-0 input tensor, ndims == 0, so the argument is -1, outside the domain. The call executes before any protective check, so the admitted set of every prior guard is trivially satisfied; this is a confirmed out-of-bounds read of TensorShape dimension storage (CWE-125), capable of crashing or leaking adjacent memory.

Valid indices for rhs's dimension list are [0, rhs.dims()); rhs.dims() == ndims is only enforced at line 12, after this read. Witness: input rank 3, rhs rank 2, so the argument ndims - 1 == 2 equals rhs's dimension count (index == capacity, one past the last valid index 1). No guard precedes line 6, so the witness passes every guard on the path; this is a second confirmed out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) on the right-hand side's dimension storage.

assumptions: Tensor::dims() returns the rank (number of dimensions), and Tensor::dim_size(d) is valid only for 0 <= d < dims(); both follow from the fragment's own usage: ndims = input.dims() at line 4 and the guard ndims >= 2 before input.dim_size(ndims - 2) at lines 17-21.
Inputs supplied via context->input(0)/input(1) are op inputs whose shapes (rank and dim sizes) are externally controllable; the fragment imposes no rank constraint before lines 5-6.
limitations: The exact byte offset of the out-of-bounds read depends on TensorShape's internal storage layout, which is not visible in the fragment; the confirmed fact is the out-of-domain index (-1, or an index >= rhs.dims()) at the call site.
In debug/DCHECK builds the same flaw may manifest as a reachable abort (CWE-617) rather than a raw read; that manifestation is not visible in the shown code and is not reported as a separate CWE.

The batch loops (lines 98, 112, 176, 196) declare int batch while batch_size (line 73) is int64; signed-overflow/non-termination would require batch_size >= 2^31, and the fragment neither establishes nor rules out such a tensor, so this is unconfirmed.

int64 n is implicitly narrowed where passed to int parameters of Getrf/Getrs/GetrfBatched/GetrsBatched (lines 105, 115, 183, 199); exploitation would require n > INT_MAX, which is not demonstrated by the shown code.
All memcpy calls (lines 67-69, 138-140, 213-215) copy NumElements-based byte counts between buffers of provably equal NumElements; no overflow or undersize is confirmed.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable from the fragment. Every EXIF-derived read/write path is bounded by named guards with exact admitted ranges: q <= exif+length-12 (line 610) caps inline 4-byte reads and the sub-IFD 4-byte read at line 827; dir_offset+number_bytes <= length (lines 640-643) caps offset-form reads; the string case re-checks p+number_bytes <= exif+length (line 733); the macro clamp (lines 40-41) keeps all FormatLocaleString writes inside the declared char buffer[MaxTextExtent]. The only suspicious call, FormatLocaleString(key, MaxTextExtent, "%s", description) at lines 785-786, writes into a buffer whose allocation size (AcquireString(property)) and the value of MaxTextExtent are not visible in the fragment, so an out-of-bounds write cannot be grounded here and is recorded as a limitation.

assumptions: exif points to a length-byte region whose end is exif+length; this is the bound every guard in the fragment uses (length=GetStringInfoLength(profile), line 529; length >= 16 enforced at line 549).
property is a NUL-terminated ISO-C string (strlen used at lines 447, 482) with strlen(property) > 5 after whitespace stripping (lines 447-448).

ReadPropertyByte/ReadPropertyUnsignedShort/ReadPropertySignedLong/ReadPropertySignedShort consume their declared byte widths and, for ReadPropertyByte, decrement length; this is the name-implied contract the fragment's guard arithmetic relies on.
MaxTextExtent is a positive compile-time constant (char buffer[MaxTextExtent], line 649); its numeric value is not shown.
tag_bytes[format] is in {1,1,2,4,8,1,1,2,4,8,4,8} for the admitted format range 1..12 (lines 617-620, 435).
AcquireQuantumMemory(number_bytes+1) succeeds or returns NULL; both outcomes are handled (lines 663-665, 737-739).
limitations: Candidate C3 (heap OOB write at FormatLocaleString(key, MaxTextExtent, "%s", description), lines 785-786): the destination capacity is set by AcquireString(property) (line 763), whose allocation size is not visible, and the size argument MaxTextExtent's value is not visible. A witness (e.g., property="exif:*" giving a 7-byte key with a >7-byte table description) would require both premises to hold; under the shown code the capacity is not identifiable, so no CWE is assigned.
The numeric value of MaxTextExtent is unknown, so the macro byte-account (lines 38-45) is proven only symbolically (writes stay <= buffer[MaxTextExtent-1]).
Provenance of property and image is internal-helper; attacker control of property is not established inside the fragment.

Allocation failures (AcquireString/AcquireQuantumMemory returning NULL then being passed to FormatLocaleString) are unchecked in the line 785 path but are allocation-failure-dependent and thus not counted as findings.
Very large components values (up to 2^31-1) are absorbed by the length screen at line 642 unless the profile itself were that large; no resource-exhaustion path is demonstrated.

Potential 32-bit size_t wrap of components*tag_bytes[format] (line 624) is partially screened at line 626 and the corrupted magnitude is then bounded by line 642; no confirmed wrap reaching a security-relevant sink.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable from the shown fragment. The nearest candidate is the trailing-space trim loop at line 21, which evaluates VIM_ISWHITE(*(bd->textstart + s - 1)) before the s > 0 operand of &&, so when s reaches 0 (textlen == 0, or an all-whitespace text) it reads bd->textstart[-1], one byte before the text span the fragment itself establishes; this is a CWE-125 candidate, but the backing allocation and capacity of bd->textstart are not declared in the shown code, so the OOB cannot be confirmed. All writes to the destination stay within the shown allocation at lines 7-8, the alloc NULL result is handled at lines 8-9, and the trim loop provably terminates.

assumptions: alloc(n) at line 7 returns a buffer of exactly the stated expression's bytes and NULL on failure, so the destination capacity is startspaces + endspaces + textlen + 1 bytes (lines 7-8).
vim_memset and mch_memmove write exactly the byte count given in their size argument (lines 11, 13, 15).
&& at line 21 short-circuits left-to-right, so the loop body executes only when both operands are true.
(*mb_head_off)(...) at line 23 returns a non-negative offset, so s strictly decreases by at least 1 per iteration.
VIM_ISWHITE reads the single byte of its argument (line 21).
limitations: Condition-operand-order issue at line 21: while (VIM_ISWHITE(*(bd->textstart + s - 1)) && s > 0) dereferences textstart + s - 1 for s == 0, yielding bd->textstart[-1]. Reachable with bd->textlen == 0 or an all-whitespace text (witnesses pass every guard on the path because the s > 0 operand cannot protect the earlier dereference). This is one byte outside the only region the fragment establishes, but the backing allocation/capacity of bd->textstart is not declared in the shown code, so the OOB read (CWE-125) is unconfirmable per the capacity-grounding rule.

struct block_def field types are not shown, so integer wrap of the line-7 allocation sum (CWE-190/195) and negative-size-to-size_t casts (CWE-195) at lines 11, 13, 15 cannot be confirmed; conversely their non-negativity cannot be established, which also weakens the safe verdict on the destination writes.

y_current->y_array size and y_current NULL status are not shown, so the line 10 store y_current->y_array[y_idx] = pnew cannot be confirmed as OOB (CWE-787) or a NULL dereference (CWE-476), and no NULL producer exists in the shown path.

The source region for mch_memmove (bd->textstart, bd->textlen bytes) at line 13 and the backward scan of mb_head_off at line 23 may extend before bd->textstart if the text begins mid-character; the backing allocation is not shown, so this is also unconfirmable.

The mb_head_off return value is treated as non-negative; if it were ever negative, line 23 could increase s and break loop termination, but no shown statement establishes a negative-return possibility.

verdict.summary: Rank-1 sparse inputs make group_dims empty (line 46), so the loop at lines 50-53 adds no dims and output_shape stays rank-0; line 65 then constructs output_strides with 0 elements and line 66 writes output_strides[output_shape.dims() - 1] == output_strides[-1] (index -1 converts to a huge size_t), an 8-byte heap out-of-bounds write before the vector buffer. The only guard before the sink (output_elements > 0, lines 55-58) admits this path (rank-0 num_elements == 1) and does not bound the stride-vector index; the loc guards only protect output_t writes downstream.

evidence.reason: Attacker-supplied shape tensors (lines 10, 13) with one element produce rank-1 TensorShapes (lines 21-28); line 46 declares group_dims with truth_st_shape.dims()-1 == 0 elements, so lines 50-53 add no dims and output_shape keeps dims()==0. Line 65 declares std::vector<int64_t> output_strides(output_shape.dims()) with capacity 0, and line 66 indexes it with output_shape.dims()-1 == -1 (int), converted to a huge size_t for unchecked std::vector::operator[], writing 8 bytes (one int64) immediately before the vector buffer: heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The only preceding guard, output_elements > 0 at lines 55-58, admits the path (num_elements()==1 for the rank-0 shape) and constrains only element count, not dims() or the stride index; the loc guards at lines 91-96 etc. occur after the sink.

assumptions: TensorShape default construction yields a rank-0 shape and TensorShape::num_elements() returns 1 for rank-0 shapes (TF scalar semantics), letting the output_elements>0 guard at line 55 pass on the witness path; this is a library invariant not derivable from the fragment.
std::vector::operator[] performs no bounds checking (standard C++ release semantics).
TensorShape::dims() returns int, so dims()-1 evaluates to -1 for a rank-0 shape and converts to size_t at the vector subscript.
Shape-tensor values are assumed to make TensorShapeUtils::MakeShape succeed; the fragment shows no rank>=2 requirement.
limitations: ValidateShapes (lines 15-18) and sparse::SparseTensor::Create (lines 35-42) are not shown; the witness assumes they admit rank-1 inputs because no visible statement rejects them. If either rejects rank-1 shapes, the line-66 OOB is unreachable; this caps confidence at 0.6.
The witness to line 66 requires output_elements==1 for a rank-0 output_shape; if TensorShape::num_elements() returned 0 instead, guard line 55 would reject the path.

A rank-0 shape tensor would make line 46's group_dims(truth_st_shape.dims()-1) underflow to a huge size_t and throw std::length_error; TF exception-to-error handling is unshown, so this is not a separate confirmed finding.

int64 overflow in output_strides[d+1]*dim_size(d+1) (line 68) and in std::inner_product (lines 89-90, 104-105, 118-119, 134-135, 152-153) is undefined behavior for huge dims, but every output_t write is guarded to loc in [0, output_elements), so memory stays in bounds; overflow could only misplace results (correctness), so an integer-overflow finding is demoted.
output_elements = output_shape.num_elements() (line 54) could itself overflow for huge dims; TensorShape internals are unshown, so guard semantics on wrapped values are unverifiable.

output_t(loc) /= truth_seq.size() (line 99): float division by zero yields inf/NaN rather than memory corruption, whether an empty group can exist is an unshown SparseTensor invariant, and normalize_ is an unshown member variable.
gtl::LevenshteinDistance is O(m*n) per matched group, i.e., polynomial in input size; no exponential blowup is derivable, so algorithmic-complexity is not confirmed.

hypothesis_st_shape.dim_size(d) at line 51 assumes equal hypothesis/truth ranks; equal ranks are not established in the fragment, but TensorShape::dim_size internals are unshown, making any rank-mismatch claim unconfirmable.

verdict.summary: All indexed accesses in the fragment are bounded by explicit guards: rank-2 for a_indices (line 3), rank-1 for a_values/a_shape (lines 8-9), a_shape element count == ndims (line 23), a_shape->NumElements() == b->dims() (line 27), and strict loop bounds at lines 33, 45, and 46 that admit only indices in [0, capacity). The sparse-index validity check at line 48 rejects both negative and out-of-range indices. No confirmed vulnerability exists within the shown code; remaining concerns (NULL raw pointers, dtype matching before flat<Index>()) depend on the out-of-scope caller.

assumptions: TensorShapeUtils::IsMatrix returns true iff rank == 2 and IsVector iff rank == 1 (used at lines 3, 8-9); these are the named contracts that make dim_size(0)/dim_size(1) and NumElements()==dim_size(0) valid reads.
a_shape->flat<Index>() (line 32) exposes exactly NumElements(a_shape) elements, which equals dim_size(0) == ndims because rank 1 is established at line 9.
a_indices->flat_inner_dims<Index>() (line 43) on a rank-2 tensor preserves element count and yields the 2-D shape [dim_size(0), dim_size(1)] = [nnz, ndims], matching the loop bounds at lines 45-46.
b->dim_size(i) (lines 34, 38) is valid for 0 <= i < b->dims(), the exact range of the loop at line 33.
TensorShape dimension sizes are used consistently: nnz/ndims read at lines 16-17 are the same values compared at lines 18, 23, and used as loop bounds at lines 45-46.
limitations: The four raw const Tensor* parameters are dereferenced without NULL checks (first use at lines 3, 8, 14, 27-33); a NULL could only be supplied by an out-of-scope caller, and the shown path cannot produce NULL, so a NULL dereference is unconfirmable.

The tensors' dtype is never validated against Index before flat<Index>() (line 32) and flat_inner_dims<Index>() (line 43); callee behavior on a dtype mismatch (data misinterpretation or a callee-internal type check/abort) and the caller's ability to deliver such a tensor are both outside the fragment.

Downstream consumption of the validated idx values (indexing the dense tensor) occurs after this function returns and is not shown; the guard at line 48 fully validates indices within the fragment's own scope.

The validation loops run O(nnz * ndims) iterations with bounds read from already-allocated tensors (lines 16-17); this is inherent to the operation and no allocation or unbounded growth occurs in the fragment, so no resource-exhaustion finding is reported.

The error path at line 54 streams the entire a_shape_flat into the error string; any log-message amplification would depend on framework error text handling not shown here and is not confirmed as a distinct vulnerability.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. Every length passed to EVP_DigestUpdate is either pinned by the equality assertion at line 13 (hash_length == SHA256_DIGEST_LENGTH={32}) before the line 16 read from a buffer with capacity EVP_MAX_MD_SIZE, derived from the same object as the pointer (hash.size()*sizeof(value_type) at lines 22-23 and 29-30), or an object/std::string extent (crl.length() at line 46, empty case excluded by line 45). All return codes are asserted before further use, and no attacker-directed value reaches a memory, injection, crypto, or status-handling failure within the fragment.

assumptions: EVP_MAX_MD_SIZE (line 2) is the BoringSSL maximum-digest-output constant; EVP_sha256() (line 11) has a fixed 32-byte output, so X509_digest writes exactly 32 bytes into hash_buffer for every admitted ca_cert_.
The residual range of hash_length after the line 13 assertion is exactly {32} (SHA256_DIGEST_LENGTH).

For the range loops (lines 20-25, 27-32), hash.size()*sizeof(std::remove_reference<decltype(hash)>::type::value_type) equals the byte extent of the array hash.data() points to, by construction, for any concrete element type.
crl is a std::string (line 44): data() is valid for length() bytes, and line 45 excludes the empty case, so line 46 reads exactly crl.length() bytes.
limitations: The concrete types of verify_certificate_hash_list_, verify_certificate_spki_list_, verify_trusted_ca_, and config_ are not shown; e.g., a span pointing into storage whose lifetime had ended would be an unconfirmable use-after-free, not derivable from this fragment.

Hashing object representations (verify_trusted_ca_, allow_expired, trust_chain_verification, only_leaf_crl) may include padding bytes; this affects digest determinism only and demonstrates no security mechanism.

RELEASE_ASSERT(rc == 1) abort sites (lines 12, 17, 24, 31, 35, 41, 47, 52, 56, 60) are not findings: a CWE-617 verdict would require an attacker-directed value admitted by the shown guards, whereas failures here stem from operator-supplied config and library/allocation failures.
A session-resumption authz bypass from an incomplete session-id digest cannot be confirmed because the fragment cannot establish which settings are missing.
The numeric value of EVP_MAX_MD_SIZE is not in the fragment; the write bound at line 11 relies on the SHA-256 API contract (32-byte output).

verdict.summary: The global-entries loop uses an unchecked, attacker-controlled u32 count: global_entry_count is read from the bitstream at line 35 and no statement bounds it against the remaining box size (unlike the sibling check at line 14 for entry_count). Each admitted iteration performs a heap allocation (line 37) and a list insert (line 39) before any per-iteration budget check, so a crafted box (e.g., global_entry_count = 0xFFFFFFFF and a large claimed size) drives ~214 million or more gf_malloc/gf_list_insert operations (~4-11 GB of heap), causing memory/CPU exhaustion / denial of service (CWE-770).

evidence.reason: Sink: per-iteration heap allocation bounded only by global_entry_count (read at line 35, gf_bs_read_u32, residual range 0..2^32-1 with no fragment-imposed constraint; the only count-vs-size guard, line 14, protects entry_count only). Witness: global_entry_count = 0xFFFFFFFF, global_entries = 1 (line 33 taken), entry_count = 0 (passes line 14), long_ids = long_offsets = 0: the loop admits i = 0..0xFFFFFFFE and each iteration consumes a minimum of 20 bytes of claimed budget (lines 41 + 48 + 57), sustaining ~214,748,364 allocations for a 0xFFFFFFFF claimed box size, or up to 2^32-1 if ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE does not enforce. malloc at line 37 runs before any per-iteration budget decree (lines 41/48/57), so allocation volume is attacker-controlled (CWE-770, uncontrolled resource allocation / DoS).

Sink: one list node inserted per admitted iteration of the loop at line 36, whose bound is the unconstrained attacker-controlled global_entry_count (line 35). The same witness (global_entry_count = 0xFFFFFFFF passing every shown guard) produces ~2.1e8+ list insertions, compounding the CWE-770 memory-exhaustion mechanism of the primary sink at lines 36-37; the return value is also discarded (lines 20/39), with no status handling.

assumptions: ptr->size is the remaining box budget, attacker-influenced via the file box header (read outside the fragment); the fragment imposes no constraint on it, and its declared type is not shown.

ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE decrements the box budget by its visible argument; whether it also returns on insufficient budget is not shown. The finding holds under both interpretations: with enforcement, iterations scale as claimed_budget/20; without it, iterations reach the full u32 count.
Byte totals for GF_GlobalAfraEntry use only the field widths visible in the fragment (lines 41-59: 8+2+2+4+4 = 20 bytes minimum per entry, plus unknown allocator/list overhead).
limitations: An out-of-bounds bitstream read would require confirming the unshown internals of gf_bs_read_* and ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE (buffer bounds, EOF behavior); unconfirmed, no CWE attached.
gf_list_insert return values (lines 20, 39) are discarded; its failure semantics and any OOB behavior for index i are not shown and were not asserted.

Loop 1 (entry_count) is not a finding: line 14 caps iterations at trunc(size/12 or /16) and the per-iteration reads (lines 22-29) match those divisors exactly; its allocation volume is linear in the claimed remaining size.
No NULL-dereference, integer-wraparound, or format/injection sink is derivable from the shown fragment.
Severity is high for a memory-exhaustion denial of service in a media parser; no RCE mechanism was identified in the fragment.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown fragment. Byte-level accounting against the allocation at line 7 proves every write fits exactly (memsets at lines 11/15, memmove at line 13, NUL at line 27 within [0, S-1]); the trailing-space loop executes only after line 6 zeroes bd->endspaces, so its reads stay within the textlen-byte region the fragment itself consumes at line 13 and it terminates because s strictly decreases (line 23). Candidates requiring negative or huge bd member values, or an out-of-range y_idx, are unconfirmable because member types, value producers, and the y_array capacity are not shown in the fragment.

assumptions: alloc's NULL-on-failure contract is visible in the fragment via the explicit == NULL check at line 8 and return FAIL at line 9.
The fragment treats [bd->textstart, bd->textstart + bd->textlen) as a readable/copyable region, evidenced by mch_memmove(pnew, bd->textstart, (size_t)bd->textlen) at line 13.
vim_memset/mch_memmove length arguments are byte counts and the allocation size at line 7 is in bytes, matching the pointer arithmetic on char_u* at lines 12/14/16/24.

Byte-level verification assumes the non-negative domain for bd->startspaces, bd->endspaces, and bd->textlen that makes the (size_t) casts at lines 11/13/15 value-preserving; the non-negativity itself is a caller/struct contract not declared inside this fragment.
mb_head_off returns a non-negative byte offset (name/usage implied by line 23), which grounds the loop-termination argument.
limitations: Signed-to-unsigned conversion (CWE-195 candidate): if any of bd->startspaces, bd->endspaces, or bd->textlen were negative, the (size_t) casts at lines 11/13/15 would pass huge lengths to vim_memset/mch_memmove and cause heap OOB writes/reads; no shown statement produces or excludes such values, and struct block_def's member types are not visible in the fragment, so no in-domain witness exists.

y_current->y_array[y_idx] = pnew (line 10) is a store through an unvalidated long y_idx, but the capacity of y_array is not identifiable from the fragment, so the OOB index claim (CWE-787) is unconfirmable.

The alloc-size expression bd->startspaces + bd->endspaces + bd->textlen + 1 (line 7) could theoretically overflow, but the member types and the magnitudes needed are unshown, so no concrete overflow witness can be derived within the fragment.

Termination and bounds of the loop at lines 21-25 rely on mb_head_off returning a non-negative offset; a negative return would make s grow, but no such contract is shown or refutable from the fragment, so this is at most an unconfirmed robustness concern.

Line 6 mutates caller state (bd->endspaces = 0) even when alloc fails at line 7-9 and the function returns FAIL; this is a behavioral state-integrity concern with no security-relevant sink in the fragment.

verdict.summary: TfLiteIntArrayCreate validates only alloc_size with `alloc_size <= 0`; since alloc_size is the unsigned type size_t, the check is equivalent to `alloc_size == 0` (line 3). An attacker-controlled negative or oversized int `size` (unconstrained by any shown statement) is therefore not rejected and flows into the byte-size computation (line 2), whose result reaches malloc (line 4) and is stored as the element count (line 6) — a signed-to-unsigned conversion of a negative value into a huge/wrapped allocation size that bypasses the only validation, enabling an undersized allocation relative to the recorded count and heap-overflow potential (CWE-195; downstream OOB write not demonstrable from the fragment).

evidence.reason: Sink: malloc consumes alloc_size, which derives at line 2 from `size` whose residual range is the FULL signed int domain [-2^31, 2^31-1] (no shown statement constrains it). The only guard, line 3 (`alloc_size <= 0` on the unsigned `size_t` declared at line 2), is equivalent to `alloc_size == 0` and admits every value in [1, 2^64-1], including huge/wrapped nonzero byte counts produced by signed-to-unsigned conversion of negative counts. The shown code therefore passes an unvalidated, potentially negative size argument into the byte-size computation and forwards the resulting unwarranted allocation size to malloc (CWE-195 mechanism); its guard's admitted set is the entire nonzero range and provides no bound protecting the allocation.

Sink: the unvalidated `int size` (full domain, no constraint in the shown code) is written into the returned object's element-count field, while the backing allocation (line 4) was sized from a byte count that the vacuous line-3 guard (`== 0` on unsigned size_t) could not filter for negative inputs. The object returned at line 7 is thus handed back with an unvalidated/corrupted element count and a potentially undersized allocation; only the NULL check at line 5 guards this write, and it cannot exclude an undersized non-NULL allocation. This is the same CWE-195 validation-bypass mechanism; an actual out-of-bounds byte count for the write itself is not confirmable because the struct layout and helper mapping are not shown.

assumptions: `alloc_size` is the unsigned type `size_t` as declared at line 2, so `alloc_size <= 0` (line 3) is semantically `alloc_size == 0`.
`TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes` takes an element count and returns a byte count (per its name and use at lines 2/4); its body is not part of the fragment.
`ret->size` is an `int`-sized field at offset 0 of TfLiteIntArray (struct definition not shown); int is 4 bytes and size_t is 64-bit on the analyzed target.
`malloc` reports failure via NULL, which the fragment handles at line 5.
limitations: The exact byte count produced by TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes for a negative/large `size` is not visible, so the finding rests on residual-range analysis (negative counts are not excluded and convert to huge/wrapped unsigned sizes) rather than a single pinned wrapped value; a helper that normalizes all invalid counts to 0 would make the line-3 guard effective for the zero outcome.

An out-of-bounds write at line 6 or in the caller-populated `data[]` region cannot be byte-exactly confirmed: the target capacity (`sizeof(TfLiteIntArray)`) and the helper's byte-count mapping are not identifiable from the fragment; no CWE-787/CWE-122 is attached for that reason.
Any memory corruption occurring after the fragment (write into `data[]` by callers based on `ret->size`) is out of scope of the shown code.

verdict.summary: Stack-based buffer overflow in check_attestation_fido_u2f: the lengths rpid_hash_len, credential_id_len, cert_x_len, and cert_y_len are entry-point inputs with no shown bounds, and they are used directly as memcpy counts into the 200-byte stack buffer data_signed (line 9). With e.g. rpid_hash_len=32, credential_id_len=100, cert_x_len=32, cert_y_len=32, the final memcpy at line 117 writes indices 198..229, overflowing by 30 bytes with attacker-influenced content, enabling stack memory corruption.

evidence.reason: cert_y_len is an entry-point size_t parameter with full unsigned domain (no shown constraint in the fragment). A witness rpid_hash_len=32, credential_id_len=100, cert_x_len=32, cert_y_len=32 passes every guard on the path (2-entry map at line 24, x5c array of size 1 at line 48, gnutls/o_base64/digest success at lines 55/72/77/82/87, sig bytestring at line 93); offsets accumulate to 198 by line 116, so this memcpy writes indices 198..229 while data_signed[200] (line 9) admits only 0..199 — a 30-byte stack overflow (CWE-121) with input-derived content.

rpid_hash_len is an entry-point size_t parameter with no bound established in the shown code. A single-parameter witness rpid_hash_len=300 passes all guards on the path (lines 24, 48, 55, 72, 77, 82, 87, 93) and makes this memcpy write indices 1..300 into data_signed[200] (line 9, capacity indices 0..199), overflowing by 101 bytes immediately at the first unbounded copy (CWE-121 stack-based buffer overflow).

assumptions: data_signed is declared as unsigned char data_signed[200] at line 9, so its valid index range is 0..199; every boundary claim is grounded in this declaration.
The length parameters credential_id_len, cert_x_len, cert_y_len, rpid_hash_len are size_t (unsigned) as declared at line 1; the fragment imposes no upper bound on any of them.
client_data_hash_len is fixed at 32 (line 10) against client_data_hash[32] (line 9); the digest step at line 87 is treated as producing 32 bytes, and the SHA-256 output length is 32.
limitations: Potential OOB read at line 87 (o_strlen on client_data) if the caller's buffer is not NUL-terminated: the fragment shows no termination statement, so termination is a caller-domain invariant, unconfirmed.
Line 36 passes cbor_string_length(key) (size_t) as the %.*s precision (int) via varargs; truncation to int is only harmful for strings > INT_MAX bytes — exotic, not confirmed as a finding.

Line 60 compares json_object_get(j_params, "root-ca-list") against json_null(), so a missing key (NULL) is treated as present; the security impact depends on the unshown body of validate_certificate_from_root.

No vulnerability is reported for the remaining code paths: the line 28-47 loop is bounded by cbor_map_size(att_stmt)==2 (line 24) so i stays in {0,1}; error/status returns in the shown fragment are checked before their dependent operations; the signature verification at line 127 uses GNUTLS_SIGN_ECDSA_SHA256.

verdict.summary: No exploitable flaw is confirmable from the fragment alone. Entry-derived start/delete are clamped to [0,length] and [0,length-start] (lines 26, 32, 42), all counters are int64 (line 4), the final length is bounded by the NJS_MAX_LENGTH check at line 47, args reads stay within the nargs-entry buffer the fragment itself indexes, and every loop terminates with exact iteration counts. The raw buffer writes (lines 62, 83, 121-122) and the delete-sized allocation (line 54) cannot be proven out of bounds because the capacities of array->start and deleted->start, and the callee parameter contracts of njs_array_alloc/njs_object_length, are not visible in the fragment; those cases belong in limitations rather than findings.

assumptions: args holds at least nargs entries: the fragment itself indexes njs_arg(args, nargs, 1) (line 21), njs_arg(args, nargs, 2) (line 37), and args[3..3+items-1] via memcpy (lines 121-122) and &args[i] (line 145) with i < nargs, so those reads are within the buffer the code itself relies on.
All derived size/index variables (start, length, items, delta, delete, i, n) are declared int64_t (line 4), so the shown arithmetic and loop counters cannot wrap in the fragment's own types.
start ∈ [0, length] by the clamp at line 26; delete ∈ [0, length - start] by lines 32 and 42; consequently start + delete ≤ length and start + items ≤ length + delta hold on every path.
The check at line 47 admits only length + delta ≤ NJS_MAX_LENGTH, and the final length stores (lines 115, 151) write that bounded value.
limitations: OOB claims for the raw buffer writes at lines 62, 83, and 121-122 are unconfirmable: the capacities of array->start and deleted->start are never declared/allocated in the fragment, so no capacity line exists to measure any excess against (no CWE).

If a slow this (line 65 branch) had length ≥ 2^32 and njs_array_alloc's length parameter truncated the int64 delete (line 54), the loops at lines 68-86 could write past a smaller deleted->start; the pure-delete shape (line 32) makes line 47 pass (length + delta = start). Both the callee parameter width and njs_object_length's length cap are outside the fragment, so this cannot be confirmed as CWE-787 under the fragment-only rule.

length (line 16) is only checked for ret == NJS_ERROR (line 17); if njs_object_length could return another non-OK status, length would be used uninitialized — the callee's return-value contract is not shown, so this is unconfirmed.
A failed property write to the fresh deleted array (line 76, only NJS_ERROR checked) or a NJS_DECLINED read absence (lines 81-84) is a semantic gap, not a shown memory-safety issue.

Splice on a slow array-like with a huge length performs O(length) property operations (lines 68-86, 134-139); the fragment imposes no shown cap on the input length, but this is an algorithmic-cost/robustness concern, not a confirmed memory-safety or injection finding.

verdict.summary: xml_parse_node recurses with no depth bound at lines 24, 40, and 83, so an attacker-controlled XML document with many processing instructions/comments or deep element nesting drives unbounded stack growth and stack exhaustion (CWE-674). Independently, the attribute loop at lines 53-66 does not advance when whitespace follows the tag name (line 56's get_until_chr stops at the delimiter without consuming it, as the fragment's own follow-up tests at lines 57/68 require), producing a non-terminating loop with unbounded attribute allocation (CWE-835).

evidence.reason: Unbounded recursion (CWE-674). scanner->curptr is entry-point XML data with no length or depth cap imposed anywhere in the fragment. Input '<a><a>...<a>' nested D times passes line 8 ('<' admitted), line 12 ('?' excluded), line 28 ('<!' excluded), line 53 (skipped, curptr at '>'), line 76 (get_char '>'), and line 80 (admitted '<' with next char neither '/' nor '!'), recursing at line 83 after consuming exactly 3 bytes per level; depth = floor(L/3) for input length L, unbounded. No depth counter exists between lines 79 and 85; PJ_CHECK_STACK() at line 6 is not a depth bound. Stack exhaustion on sufficiently large L is the standard CWE-674 impact.

Same unbounded-recursion mechanism (CWE-674) via processing-instruction constructs: each '<?x?>' consumes 5 bytes through lines 13-23 and then unconditionally recurses at line 24 with no depth limit; for L attacker-controlled bytes, depth >= L/5, e.g. 100,000 consecutive PIs produce 100,000 stack frames.

Same unbounded-recursion mechanism (CWE-674) via comment constructs: the comment loop at lines 29-39 terminates, then line 40 recurses with no depth bound, so N consecutive '<!--...-->' comments yield N stack frames.

Non-terminating loop with unbounded allocation (CWE-835). The only progress in this loop is line 56, whose name-implied semantics (stop at the delimiter without consuming it - required by the fragment's own tests at lines 57 and 68, which inspect *scanner->curptr immediately after get_until_chr) mean it cannot advance when curptr already sits on a delimiter. Witness '': line 50 stops at the space (space is in its delimiter set " />\t\r\n"), line 53 admits the space (' ' != '>' and ' ' != '/'), line 56 stops at ' ' (in "=> \t\r\n") with an empty name and unchanged curptr, line 57 rejects (' ' != '='), line 65 pushes a fresh attr from line 54, and the loop re-tests the identical state forever, exhausting both CPU and memory. No whitespace skip, iteration cap, or EOF test exists between lines 53 and 66.

assumptions: scanner->curptr is the attacker-supplied XML character stream consumed by this parser; the fragment imposes no input length cap, so recursion depth and loop-iteration counts are unresolved over their residual domains.

pj_scan_get_until_chr / pj_scan_get_until_ch stop at (and do not consume) the first delimiter character; the fragment's own follow-up tests at lines 57, 68, and 117 inspect *scanner->curptr immediately after such a call, so stop-at-delimiter is required for the shown control flow to work at all.
Stack size and per-frame size are not shown in the fragment; the stack-exhaustion impact follows from unbounded recursion depth and is the standard consequence of CWE-674.
limitations: Out-of-bounds reads of *scanner->curptr and *(scanner->curptr+1) (lines 8, 12, 17, 53, 80-81, 93) cannot be confirmed because the scanner buffer's capacity and EOF representation are not declared in the fragment.
attr->value.slen -= 2 (line 62) can corrupt the attribute length when fewer than two quote bytes were consumed, but no consumer of attr->value appears in the fragment, so the impact is unconfirmable.
NULL dereference after alloc_node/alloc_attr (lines 44, 54) lacks an allocation-failure producer in the shown code.

Return states of pj_scan_get_char / pj_scan_get_until_ch / pj_scan_get_until_chr / pj_scan_get_quotes (lines 47, 50, 56, 58-59, 89, 97, 100, 110) are discarded; this is a systemic error-handling weakness (CWE-754 pattern), but a concrete failure path requires callee error semantics not shown.

The CDATA loop at lines 98-101 exhibits the same no-advance infinite-loop class on valid input such as '' under the same stop-at-delimiter semantics; it is folded into the CWE-835 finding rather than reported separately.
The exact input length that exhausts the stack depends on runtime stack configuration (not shown); the finding is demonstrated as unbounded depth, not a specific byte count.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The byte-accumulation loop into command (lines 108-120) is provably bounded: the line 116-118 guard admits writes only while p-command <= MaxTextExtent-2, so the data write at line 115 never exceeds index MaxTextExtent-2 and the NUL at line 119 never exceeds index MaxTextExtent-1 of the MaxTextExtent-element array declared at line 9. No injection is reachable (all delegate command arguments are generated unique filenames or numeric strings; formats are literal or config data). Remaining concerns (discarded ExternalDelegateCommand status at line 223, attacker-controlled negative box coordinates producing huge page dimensions at lines 153-154, unchecked AcquireUniqueFilename return at line 215) have security impact only in callees and delegates outside the fragment and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: MaxTextExtent is the positive compile-time array capacity used identically in the declarations (lines 9, 11, 12, 14) and in the loop guard (line 117); the safety argument requires MaxTextExtent >= 2, which the guard arithmetic (MaxTextExtent-1) presupposes.
FormatLocaleString and CopyMagickString honor the explicit capacity argument passed at each call site (lines 168, 188, 191, 196, 204, 208, 214, 216, 245).
LocaleNCompare reads at most n bytes and stops at the first NUL, so command (NUL-terminated at line 119) is read safely by the prefix checks at lines 124, 126, 137.
sscanf on the NUL-terminated in-memory command returns a value in 0..4 (no EOF path), and the conversions at lines 131-135, 142-146 write exactly into the four double fields of bounds.
AcquireUniqueSymbolicLink and AcquireUniqueFilename produce generated, metacharacter-free unique path names in the provided buffers (callee contract by name; behavior not shown in the fragment).
DefaultResolution and PSDensityGeometry resolve to positive finite density values, so delta.x/delta.y are non-zero at lines 192-195.
SyncNextImageInList returns NULL at the end of a list, which the do/while loop at lines 243-257 relies on for termination (callee semantics not shown).
limitations: Demoted OOB candidate: the accumulator loop (lines 108-120) cannot overflow command because the guard at lines 116-118 evaluates after the increment and admits continuation only while p-command <= MaxTextExtent-2; the largest data index written is MaxTextExtent-2 and the NUL flush index is MaxTextExtent-1 for the MaxTextExtent-element array declared at line 9.

Demoted injection candidate: the delegate command built at lines 216-220 and executed at line 223 contains no attacker-controlled shell metacharacters — density (line 188) and options (lines 196-197) are numeric strings, and read_info->filename/input_filename are generated unique paths (lines 215, 70); the format string itself is config data from GetDelegateCommands (line 217).

Demoted status-handling candidate (CWE-754 / CWE-390 class): the return of ExternalDelegateCommand (line 223) is stored in status and never used; ReadImage (line 225) then runs on the delegate-failure state. When the delegate produces no output, line 229 converts this to a clean exception; when it leaves partial output, the fragment returns a partially-decoded image, but the security consequence would materialize inside ReadImage's unshown coders, so the impact is not demonstrable within the fragment.

Demoted integer-conversion candidate (CWE-195/CWE-770 class): attacker-controlled doubles from CropBox/MediaBox (lines 131-146) can be negative (e.g., "CropBox [100 100 50 50]" gives width (size_t)(-50)), producing huge page.width/page.height (lines 153-154) that flow into the -g delegate argument (lines 196-197) and image->page (line 246); the conversion is shown, but the damaging allocation/behavior occurs in GhostPCL and downstream coders outside the fragment, so impact is unconfirmed.

Demoted error-handling candidate: the return of AcquireUniqueFilename (line 215) is discarded; on failure the content/state of read_info->filename and the effect of RelinquishUniqueFileResource (line 226) depend on callee behavior not shown in the fragment.

Unchecked allocations (AcquireImage line 63, AcquireString lines 186-187, CloneImageInfo line 199) are not NULL-checked; exploiting them requires OOM, and no security-relevant operation on the failure state is visible in the fragment.
Non-termination of the do/while loop (lines 243-257) cannot be confirmed without the body of SyncNextImageInList; standard semantics (NULL at end of list) are assumed.

The stale-count behavior (count retains its value across flushes at lines 131-148) only replays the most recently successfully parsed box in the max update at lines 155-158 and has no demonstrated security impact.
The geometry string computed at lines 168-169 is never consumed within the fragment.

verdict.summary: Both tensors' last-dimension sizes are read with index ndims-1 before the rank/rhs-rank checks execute. A rank-0 input yields index -1 into input.dim_size (capacity = input.dims() == 0), and an input rank of 3 with rhs rank 2 yields index 2 into rhs's 2-element dimension array (index == capacity). The subsequent OP_REQUIRES_ASYNC checks (ndims >= 2; rhs.dims() == ndims) run only after these reads, so each reachable path performs a bounded out-of-bounds read of TensorShape's dimension storage, which is then discarded when the op aborts.

evidence.reason: Sink L5 receives index ndims - 1 where ndims = input.dims() (L4) is entry-point input with residual range [0, INT_MAX] (no shown check precedes L5). Witness ndims == 0 (rank-0 tensor) makes the index -1; the accessed TensorShape dimension array has capacity input.dims() == 0, so -1 is out of the accessor's required domain [0, 0) by one element before the start. The rank guards at L8-L11, L12-L16 execute after this read and do not protect it; the read value is discarded when the guard aborts. Primary mechanism: out-of-bounds read via an index derived from unvalidated input (CWE-125).

Sink L6 indexes rhs with ndims - 1 taken from input's rank (L4) before any rhs-rank validation (the rhs.dims() == ndims guard is at L12-L16, after the read). Witness: input rank 3, rhs rank 2 makes the index 2 while rhs's dimension array capacity is rhs.dims() == 2, i.e., index == capacity, a read one element past the end; a rank-0 input makes the index -1 instead. Both witnesses pass every guard on the path (none precede L6). The value is discarded when the L12-L16 check aborts. Primary mechanism: out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

assumptions: TensorShape::dim_size(d) requires 0 <= d < dims(); dims() is the element count of the tensor's dimension array, so the array capacity used for grounding is the tensor's own rank obtained in the shown code (L4 for input, returned on the rhs operand of L6).
OP_REQUIRES_ASYNC/OP_REQUIRES_OK_ASYNC failures invoke done() and return, so guards at L8-L11 and L12-L16 abort the op but cannot make the earlier reads at L5-L6 safe.

Memcpy destinations have equal total element counts to their sources by construction: output uses rhs.shape() (L40), input_copy uses input.shape() (L63/L71), and transposed_rhs preserves rhs.NumElements() (L131-L134), so the memcpy sizes at L76, L147, L205 are exact.

GetScratchSpace allocations at L94, L152, L155 either succeed (buffers exist for the subsequent loops) or fail inside the framework; no shown statement handles a failure state with a security-relevant operation.
limitations: Whether dim_size performs a raw OOB read or bounds-checks with a debug CHECK is callee-internal and not shown; the confirmation rests on the accessor's name/use-imposed domain plus the tensor's own dims() capacity, so confidence is capped and the alternative (reachable CHECK failure) is not separately asserted.

Loop counters declared int compared against int64 batch_size (L105, L119, L166, L186) would overflow for batch_size >= 2^31 (requires ~2^31 * n^2 elements, ~8.6 GB for float with n=1) and the resulting behavior depends on signed-overflow UB; demoted from finding.

int64 n/nrhs/batch_size narrowing into cuSolver int parameters (L112, L122, L173, L189) is unconfirmable because the callee parameter types are not shown and the triggering sizes are astronomically large; demoted.
-host_info at L180 is undefined behavior only if the library returns host_info == INT_MIN; INT_MIN is not confirmed for any admitted input; demoted.
Unchecked GetScratchSpace allocations (L94, L152, L155) produce no security-relevant operation on a failure state; demoted per the absence rule.
No command/SQL/path/injection, crypto/entropy, temp-file, or authz surfaces exist in the fragment; not applicable.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable from the fragment. The copy at L56-L58 is guarded on the source side by the element-count equality at L48-L55, but the destination buffer 'data' has no visible capacity; the subscript sss_[idx] at L28 is only lower-bounded by CHECK_GE at L25 with no upper bound or sss_ declaration shown; the CHECK_GE abort requires a fname_to_index_/sss_ consistency invariant that is not established in the fragment; and VLOG output carries only internal-helper parameters of unknown provenance. All candidates fail capacity or reachability grounding and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: The NULL check at L14 guarantees tss is non-null wherever tss->shape() is used (L42, L57).
The equality guard at L48-L55 admits only the state where the proto element count equals shp_s.num_elements(), so the source buffer handed to the copy at L56-L58 has exactly that many elements.
The range-based loop at L21-L59 always advances its iterator, so it terminates for every input.
limitations: sss_[idx] at L28 could be an OOB read (CWE-125) if idx >= sss_.size(), but the size/capacity of the member sss_ is not declared in the fragment, and the consistency invariant between fname_to_index_ and sss_ is established outside the shown code, so the witness cannot be grounded (the only shown guard, CHECK_GE at L25, bounds only the lower end).

CopyDataFromTensorSliceToTensorSlice at L56-L58 could write out of bounds of the caller's 'data' buffer, but no size or allocation for 'data' appears in the fragment, so no excess can be computed against a quoted capacity; the callee body is not shown to derive an out-of-domain argument at the call site.

CHECK_GE at L25 can abort on idx == -1 (CWE-617) only if FindTensorSlice returns a filename in 'details' that fname_to_index_ lacks; the fragment neither establishes nor refutes that map-completeness invariant, so attacker-directed reachability of the abort is unconfirmed.

VLOG statements (L10, L29-L31, L36-L38, L44-L45, L50-L53) write 'name', slice debug strings, and computed keys into logs, but 'name' is an internal-helper parameter of unknown provenance and no log consumer / trust boundary is shown, so log injection (CWE-117) is not confirmable.

verdict.summary: The shape tensors' element count (sparse rank) is never constrained to >= 2 by any statement in the fragment. With rank 1 (e.g. hypothesis_shape = [4], truth_shape = [4]) the output TensorShape stays scalar (dims()==0), so line 66 writes output_strides[-1] into a std::vector whose capacity 0 is declared at line 65 - a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). With rank 0, line 46 computes dims()-1 == -1 as a std::vector size, becoming 2^64-1 and aborting via std::length_error (CWE-191). The output_elements > 0 check at lines 55-58 admits the scalar output shape, so it does not protect the witness path.

evidence.reason: Heap OOB write (CWE-787). The index is derived entirely from entry-point input: rank = NumElements() of the shape tensors (lines 24, 28) flows to group_dims.size() at line 46, then to output_shape.dims() (no AddDim runs at lines 50-53 when rank==1), leaving output_shape scalar with dims()==0. Capacity: std::vector<int64_t> output_strides(output_shape.dims()) at line 65 is a 0-element vector on the witness path (shape tensors each containing one int64 element, e.g. [4]; every shown guard admits it: input/ValidateShapes/MakeShape/Create succeed, and output_elements==1>0 passes at lines 55-58). The index output_shape.dims()-1 == -1 converts to size_t 2^64-1 for operator[], exceeding capacity 0, so the write is out of domain by the entire object.

Integer underflow of an allocation size (CWE-191). With rank 0 (shape tensors whose NumElements()==0, e.g. a [0]-shaped int64 tensor), MakeShape at lines 26-28 yields a scalar TensorShape with dims()==0, so dims()-1 == -1 is implicitly converted to std::vector<int64_t>::size_type (2^64-1); the vector constructor then throws std::length_error/bad_alloc, which is uncaught and terminates the process. No statement in the fragment imposes a minimum on the shape tensors' NumElements(), and the opaque ValidateShapes call at lines 15-18 cannot supply one.

assumptions: TensorShapeUtils::MakeShape(data, ndims, &shape) with ndims==0 creates a scalar TensorShape with dims()==0 (standard library/framework contract of the shown call at lines 21-28).
TensorShape::num_elements() of a 0-dim scalar shape is 1, so the guard at lines 55-58 admits the scalar output shape.

std::vector<int64_t> construction and operator[] follow the C++ standard library semantics; the index at line 66 is out of domain whether dims() is signed (0-1 == -1 cast to size_t) or unsigned (wrap to SIZE_MAX).
ValidateShapes at lines 15-18 is treated as imposing no constraint because its body is absent from the fragment; per the task rules its unshown invariants cannot be used in either direction.
limitations: A second OOB-write pathway through the output_t(loc) writes (lines 97/112/126/142/160): a negative loc would pass the loc < output_elements guards (91-96 etc., signed int64 comparison), but producing negative loc requires int64 overflow inside std::inner_product (lines 89-90 etc.) with extreme dim/index values and depends on unshown index-bounds validation, so no confirmed witness exists within the shown arithmetic.

The rank-0 line-46 crash additionally requires sparse::SparseTensor::Create (lines 35-42) to succeed on scalar shapes and assumes the throw is uncaught; both behaviors are outside the fragment, so this secondary finding is capped at confidence 0.8.

Rank values above INT_MAX would also reach line 66 via static_cast<int>(group_dims.size()) truncation at line 50, but that requires a >2^31-element shape tensor (16GB) and is not needed for the confirmed witness.
Allocations at lines 31 and 46 grow linearly with the input shape tensor's element count, so resource amplification is bounded by input volume; not reported as a finding.
The fragment contains no injection, crypto, entropy, authn/authz, path, or temp-file sinks; dtype enforcement for vec<int64_t>() at lines 23/27 is a framework guarantee outside the fragment.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable from the fragment alone. The input-derived skip length `off` (line 13) and the input-driven PCE copy into the fixed-capacity buffer `adts->pce_data` (lines 38-41) are the only real danger surfaces, but in both cases the out-of-domain value (off > 8*size, or a PCE bit count exceeding MAX_PCE_SIZE) cannot be derived from statements visible in the fragment: `off` is produced by an unshown parser contract, and the PCE length plus the numeric value of MAX_PCE_SIZE are not shown. The `objecttype - 1` underflow at line 14 is neutralized by the unsigned comparison at line 17. The discarded return of `ff_copy_pce_data` (line 40) can corrupt `pce_size` but no security-relevant operation consumes that value within the fragment.

assumptions: Line 7-9: success of `init_get_bits8(&gb, buf, size)` implies `gb` is initialized over `buf` with capacity 8*size bits and `size` is a valid non-negative byte count per that API's contract; the callee body is not shown.

Line 38: `MAX_PCE_SIZE` is used in the shown code as the byte capacity of `adts->pce_data` (destination argument of `init_put_bits`); neither the ADTSContext field declaration nor the numeric value of `MAX_PCE_SIZE` is shown.

Lines 14-17: `m4ac.object_type` and `adts->objecttype` are treated as (or convertible to) signed int for the arithmetic at line 14 and the unsigned comparison at line 17; their declared types are not shown.
Line 10: `avpriv_mpeg4audio_get_config2` parses `buf` of `size` bytes; its return `off` is a consumed-bit count from that parse (name-implied contract).
limitations: Potential heap OOB write into `adts->pce_data` via `ff_copy_pce_data(&pb, &gb)` (line 40): a PCE whose encoded length exceeds `MAX_PCE_SIZE` bits could overrun `put_bits`, but the PCE bit-count derivation and the numeric capacity are not in the fragment, so the write volume N and the exact excess are unconfirmable (no CWE assigned).

Potential OOB read / reachable assertion via `skip_bits_long(&gb, off)` (line 13) followed by `get_bits` (lines 25/29/33) and `ff_copy_pce_data` (line 40): `off` has residual range [0, INT_MAX] after line 11, but no in-fragment statement derives `off > 8*size`; the magnitude is determined inside the unshown parser, whose own contract binds it to the `size`-byte buffer (unconfirmable either direction).

Truncated/empty extradata (e.g., `size` too small for the four flag bits or the PCE bits) would only trigger reads/asserts inside unshown callees (`get_bits`, `ff_copy_pce_data`); failure mode and bounds behavior are not visible in the fragment.

Error-handling concern: the return of `ff_copy_pce_data` is not checked (line 40); an internal failure can store a negative `adts->pce_size` while the function returns success (lines 40, 43-44). No security-relevant in-fragment operation consumes that failure state; downstream use of `pce_size` is outside the fragment (CWE-754 unconfirmed).

Line 14 `m4ac.object_type - 1` can underflow for `object_type == 0`, but the unsigned comparison at line 17 rejects the negative result, and `objecttype` has no in-fragment sink, so this is not a finding.

verdict.summary: afra_box_read reads global_entry_count (u32) from the file at line 36 and uses it, unvalidated, as the iteration bound of a loop that allocates a GF_GlobalAfraEntry and inserts it into a list on every iteration (lines 37-38 and 61). The size gate at lines 14-15 is applied only to entry_count, never to global_entry_count, so a crafted box with global_entries=1 (line 9) and global_entry_count=0xFFFFFFFF drives up to 4,294,967,295 allocations (>=~32 bytes each plus list overhead), exhausting memory and causing a denial of service (CWE-770).

evidence.reason: global_entry_count is entry-point input read at line 36 (gf_bs_read_u32) with residual range [0, 2^32-1]; the only size gate in the fragment (lines 14-15, `ptr->size / (ptr->long_offsets ? 16 : 12) < ptr->entry_count`) constrains entry_count, not global_entry_count. The loop guard at line 37 (`i < ptr->global_entry_count`) admits the full u32 domain, so for the witness global_entries=1 (line 9, admitted by line 34), entry_count=0 (passes lines 14-15), global_entry_count=0xFFFFFFFF, this gf_malloc runs in every one of 4,294,967,295 iterations with no shown bound or early exit, causing unbounded allocation and memory exhaustion (CWE-770).

Same unvalidated global_entry_count driver (line 36 -> loop line 37): every iteration pins a newly allocated entry into the list, so memory growth is compounded by list storage (one pointer per entry, >=~34 GB at the 0xFFFFFFFF witness) and no shown constraint limits the loop volume. Same CWE-770 mechanism at a distinct sink statement.

assumptions: unsigned int i (line 3) is 32-bit and matches the u32 loop bounds, so i cannot wrap before the loops' strict `<` conditions fail (lines 17, 37).
gf_bs_read_* values are attacker-controlled entry-point data with their full declared domains; none of the loop bounds is constrained by a shown EOF/error check.

sizeof(GF_GlobalAfraEntry) is at least 32 bytes given the fields assigned at lines 41-58 (time u64, segment+fragment u32+u32, afra_offset+offset_from_afra u64+u64); impact is quantified with this size and holds for any positive size.
ptr->size (used at line 14) is an unsigned box-size field; its type is not shown, and the finding does not depend on its value or type.
limitations: ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE is not defined in the fragment; if it validates the remaining size and returns an error on underflow (semantics not visible), the global loop is instead capped by the attacker-declared box bytes (~20-32 B/entry, ~1.6-2x allocation amplification) rather than fully unbounded. The loop is treated strictly by the shown statements (count-driven).

Discarded gf_list_insert return values (lines 31, 61) could leak an entry and still report GF_OK (line 65), but this requires an unshown internal allocation failure with no security-relevant operation on the failure state; demoted.
An out-of-bounds bitstream read (CWE-125) is not confirmed: reads at lines 41-58 go through gf_bs_read_*, whose overrun/EOF behavior is not shown and whose return values are unchecked.
The local-entry loop (lines 17-32) is gated by the size check at lines 14-15; its allocation volume (up to floor(size/12) entries for a declared-u32 box) is not reported as a separate finding.
No integer-overflow or boundary finding: the arithmetic at line 14 is division/comparison of unsigned values and cannot wrap.

verdict.summary: In the sliced QuantizeV2 path, output_min_tensor/output_max_tensor are allocated with minmax_shape (the shape of attacker-supplied input_min_range), while the loop bound num_slices = input.dim_size(axis_) is taken from a different tensor and never checked against minmax_shape.numel(). A concrete input (input {2,4}, axis_=1, min/max ranges shape {1}) makes the loop index i reach 1..3 on 1-element buffers, so &output_min_tensor->flat<float>()(i) (line 53) points past the 4-byte allocation and QuantizeSlice performs a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787); the same loop also performs out-of-bounds reads min_ranges(i)/max_ranges(i) (lines 51-52).
