verdict.summary: sdb_edit forwards the unconstrained EDITOR/VISUAL environment string into system(3): the line-50 space test selects the system() branch but filters no shell metacharacters, so an editor value such as 'x; touch /tmp/pwn' executes arbitrary commands when the procedure is edited. Separately, the pid-to-filename sprintf at line 4 overflows its 14-byte heap buffer (allocated at line 3) whenever the OS assigns a 7+ digit PID, a 1-byte-plus heap out-of-bounds write.

evidence.reason: CWE-78 command injection. Taint: editor (getenv at lines 20/22) is entry-point environment data whose residual range is any C string; the only shown constraints are the NULL fallbacks (lines 21-24) and the space test at line 50, and none of them escapes, quotes, or strips shell metacharacters. The line-50 guard's admitted set for this branch is exactly 'editor contains at least one space', which is also the only precondition for reaching system(3). Witness by simulation: language==LANG_SINGULAR passes line 12; fopen/body/fork guards pass (lines 6, 27/30, 48); EDITOR='x; touch /tmp/pwn' contains a space so strchr at line 50 returns non-NULL and the else-branch is admitted; line 58 builds 'x; touch /tmp/pwn /tmp/sd000000123' into the exact-fit allocation of line 57; system(p) at line 59 runs /bin/sh, where ';' ends 'x' and the injected command executes. The sink is unbounded shell command execution as the process user.

CWE-787 heap buffer overflow. Capacity is established at line 3: omStrDup('/tmp/sd000000') yields a 14-byte buffer (13 chars + NUL, indices 0-13). The write starts at filename+7, leaving 7 bytes, so sprintf can hold at most 6 pid digits plus NUL. getpid() is OS-provided pid_t/int with no bound visible in the shown code, so 7-digit values (e.g., 1,000,000) are in the residual range: they place digits at indices 7-13 and the terminating NUL at index 14, 1 byte past the 14-byte capacity (8 bytes written into 7 available), with larger overflows for bigger PIDs. No shown statement constrains the pid before the write, and the out-of-bounds byte lands in the heap chunk allocated at line 3.

assumptions: omStrDup's name-implied contract allocates exactly strlen(source)+1 bytes, giving the line-3 buffer a 14-byte capacity (indices 0-13).
Name-implied sink semantics: sprintf writes digits plus a NUL; system executes via /bin/sh; execlp performs no shell interpretation.

The editor branch is reached only in the normal runtime flow: fopen succeeds (line 6), the procedure body becomes non-NULL (lines 27/30), and fork() returns 0 (line 48); the witness does not need to defeat those guards, which are runtime-environment conditions, not input filters.
limitations: The CWE-787 witness requires the OS to actually assign a PID of 7+ decimal digits (>= 1,000,000); pid_max is not visible in the fragment and some platforms wrap PIDs below that, so this is a sound residual-range finding rather than a platform-independent demonstrated value (confidence 0.6).

(int)len+1 at line 80 truncates for temp files > INT_MAX bytes, and an unchecked ftell()==-1 (line 76) would flow into omAlloc(0), myfread(size -1), and body[-1]='\0' at line 82; both triggers require a >2GB file or a libc stream error not producible by the shown code, so they are recorded here with no CWE.
Unchecked allocation failures (omStrDup line 25, omAlloc lines 57/80) would yield NULL and crash at strchr/system/fread; no security-relevant operation runs on that failure state in the shown code.

The predictable /tmp/sd<pid> path created with fopen(...,'w') (lines 3-5) is exposed to a local symlink/race attack (CWE-59/CWE-377 class); it is single-shot, requires local access and PID guessing, and is not independently confirmed from the fragment.
strlen(pi->data.s.body) at line 40 assumes caller-supplied bodies are NUL-terminated; the fragment does not establish that invariant.
execlp failure (line 52) is followed by Print and exit(0) (line 61), reporting success after failure, but no security-relevant operation depends on that status in the shown code.

verdict.summary: LWPolyline parsing contains two attacker-reachable heap OOB writes. (1) The group-42 branch omits the vertexIndex>=0 lower-bound guard present in the 10/20/30 branch: when a 42 record precedes the first 10 record, vertexIndex stays -1 (set at line 17), and line 34 writes vertices[4*(-1)+3] = vertices[-1], 8 bytes before the heap buffer. (2) The allocation size 4*maxVertices (line 9) is an unchecked int multiply over attacker-controlled maxVertices (line 4, only bounded below by line 5), so values >= 536870913 overflow the size and the init loop (lines 11-14) and vertex writes overflow the undersized allocation. Both are CWE-787; the size corruption is the independent CWE-190 root cause.

evidence.reason: Entry-point groupCode==42 reaches this sink with vertexIndex==-1 (set at line 17 after group code 90 with maxVertices=1, admitted by the maxVertices>0 check at line 5). The guard at line 33 (vertexIndex<maxVertices) bounds only above, so -1 passes (-1<1); the vertexIndex>=0 guard at line 30 applies only to the groupCode<=30 branch at line 29. The sink computes 4*(-1)+3 = -1, which is outside the valid index range 0..3 of the buffer allocated at line 9 (new double[4*maxVertices] with maxVertices=1, capacity 4 doubles), writing 8 bytes before the heap buffer. Primary CWE-787 heap buffer overflow via out-of-bounds (negative) index.

toInt(groupValue) (line 4) is unreserved entry-point input stored in int maxVertices; the only shown constraint is maxVertices>0 (line 5), admitting the full positive int domain. For maxVertices=1073741825 (admitted), the int expression 4*maxVertices at line 9 overflows (4294967300 wraps to 4 on 32-bit two's complement), so line 9 allocates only 4 doubles (valid indices 0..3) while this init loop, bounded at line 10 by i<maxVertices, writes vertices[i*4..i*4+3] up to 4*maxVertices-1; at i=1 this sink indexes 4, equal to the wrapped capacity, causing the first heap OOB write. Any admitted maxVertices>=536870913 makes 4*maxVertices unrepresentable and corrupts the size; lines 31 and 34 later index the same undersized allocation. CWE-787 (primary) with CWE-190 (integer overflow corrupting the allocation size) as the independent root cause.

assumptions: maxVertices, vertexIndex, and groupCode are 32-bit signed int members; the value returned by toInt(groupValue) is stored into int maxVertices and used in int arithmetic at lines 9, 25, 31, 34.
The allocation unit is double: line 9 new double[4*maxVertices] yields 4*maxVertices double elements with valid indices 0..4*maxVertices-1.
vertexIndex is set to -1 at line 17 on every admitted group code 90.
limitations: If group code 90 has not been processed before a vertex record, maxVertices/vertices are not initialized by the fragment; any finding depending on that initial state is not demonstrable from the shown code.

A double-free/use-after-free could arise if new (line 9) throws after delete[] (line 7), leaving vertices dangling for a later call; this depends on allocation failure plus later re-entry and is subsumed by the overflow finding.

Signed overflow is undefined behavior in C++; the concrete witness for the overflow finding assumes the usual 32-bit two's-complement wrap of 4*maxVertices, while the residual-range claim (unrepresentable size for all admitted maxVertices >= 536870913) holds regardless.
Behavior of toInt/toReal on non-numeric groupValue is not shown and was not treated as a finding.
Huge maxVertices also enables memory-exhaustion DoS; it is folded into the CWE-190/CWE-787 finding rather than reported separately.

verdict.summary: sdb_edit takes the EDITOR/VISUAL environment value (lines 19-24), which the fragment never constrains, and when it contains a space routes it unescaped through sprintf into system() (lines 49-58), giving an attacker full command injection (CWE-78) with a witness such as EDITOR="sh -c id". evidence.reason: CWE-78 command injection. The value survives omStrDup (line 24) and the literal format "%s %s" (line 57) with no escaping/quoting/filtering, so shell metacharacters reach system(). Witness EDITOR="sh -c id": passes line 49 (contains spaces) and reaches line 58 as "sh -c id /tmp/sdXXXXXX", executing an arbitrary shell command. The execlp branch (line 51) is not a shell, so the space-carrying payload is required and is admitted.

CWE-122 heap buffer overflow (root cause CWE-681/190 long-to-int truncation). len = ftell(fp) (line 75) has residual range [-1, LONG_MAX] with no shown cap or error check. Line 79 allocates only (int)len+1 bytes, while this call passes the untruncated long len as the read size. Witness len=4294967297 (sparse file written by the attacker-chosen editor): (int)len = 1, capacity 2 bytes (line 79), myfread writes up to 4294967297 bytes -> undersized by ~2^32-1 bytes. Guards on the path (lines 5, 11, 20-29, 43, 68) all admit this witness; no check on len exists between line 75 and this sink.

Same CWE-122 as the myfread sink: the index len is the untruncated long from line 75, but the buffer capacity is (int)len+1 from line 79. For the same witness len=4294967297 the buffer is 2 bytes and this write is at index 4294967297, a heap OOB write. No guard between line 75 and this sink constrains len.

assumptions: int is 32-bit and long is 64-bit (LP64), so (int)len truncates values > INT_MAX at line 79.
myfread follows standard fread semantics (reads up to size*nmemb bytes into ptr), and its size/length parameter is consumed as such at line 80.

limitations: The CWE-122 finding is boundary-brittle: the concrete witness requires the attacker-chosen editor to produce a file of at least 2^32 bytes (a multi-gigabyte sparse file). Confidence capped at 0.8 for that finding; the residual-range analysis (any len >= 2^32 wraps; len in [2^31, 2^32) turns (int)len negative -> huge size_t/NULL alloc; len == -1 -> omAlloc(0) with 2^64-1 read size) supports it without a single demonstrated value.

f=NULL on the int f at line 15 is a dead store with no effect; f is not used after the if/else.

TOCTOU on the /tmp file is not exploitable across users: mkstemp yields a 0600, user-owned file in sticky /tmp (line 4), and a same-uid attacker already holds the user's privileges.

File content read at lines 78-81 becomes procedure body data; no parser is shown, so code-execution via malicious body content is out of scope of this fragment.

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability is confirmed in this fragment. The function forwards the unconstrained int parameter user_tick to void subroutines (lines 6, 8) and mixes it with jiffies into per-CPU net_rand_state via a deliberate, modulus-wrapping addition (line 22). The fragment contains no memory operations, no length or index computation, no loops, no injection sinks, and never reads the mixed entropy state, so none of the demoted candidates (unvalidated forwarding, entropy-mixing adequacy) satisfies taint-and-reachability to a confirmed sink.

assumptions: current is non-NULL by the kernel invariant (derived from the running task's stack); the fragment never dereferences p (line 3, 6).
All callees in the fragment return void, so no return status is produced or discarded.
rol32 operates on 32 bits and net_rand_state.s1 is an unsigned per-CPU word, per standard kernel definitions; neither declaration is shown in the fragment.
account_process_tick and rcu_sched_clock_irq consume user_tick as a flag/count per their parameter names and call shapes; no index/size/length semantics are visible in the fragment.
limitations: The declaration of net_rand_state (type of s1) and every consumer of the mixed entropy state are outside the fragment; whether line 22 stirs it sufficiently for downstream uses cannot be confirmed here, and no weak-algorithm or weak-seed choice is visible, so no CWE-326/CWE-338 finding is attached.

user_tick is unconstrained in the fragment (no comparison or cast on lines 1-23) and is forwarded unchanged at lines 6 and 8; per the call-site rule, unmodified forwarding is not a finding, and a hazard would require a callee to treat it as an index/size, which the names do not indicate.

On 64-bit builds, rol32(jiffies, 24) at line 22 truncates the high 32 bits of jiffies; this only changes the magnitude of a deliberate mixing addend and reaches no index/size/capacity operation, so it is not a CWE-190 finding.

A negative user_tick wraps in the unsigned addition at line 22; the mod-2^32 arithmetic is the intended mixing behavior and the state is never read in the fragment, so no security-relevant corruption is demonstrated.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable from the fragment alone. The suspicious name-area path is guarded by the visible check `if(dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN)` (line 72) and by the buffer declaration `char buffer[sizeof(struct squashfs_dir_entry) + SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1]` (lines 5-6), which keep the name read (line 78) and the NUL write at index `dire->size + 1` (line 82) inside the buffer for the only confirmable (non-negative) size domain. Every candidate defect (NULL dereference of `*i` from `read_inode`, off-by-one on `dire->name`, negative `dire->size`, `dirh.count` wrap, `(*i)->data` wrap, unchecked `strdup`) depends on struct definitions, field signedness/widths, or callee contracts (`read_inode`, `read_directory_data`) that are not present in the shown code, so no three-part confirmation can be completed in either direction.

assumptions: Buffer total capacity is visible: `char buffer[sizeof(struct squashfs_dir_entry) + SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1]` (lines 5-6), with `dire = (struct squashfs_dir_entry *) buffer` (line 7).
Guard at line 72 (`if(dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN)`) excludes sizes >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN, admitting non-negative values in [0, SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN-1].
`read_directory_data` results are checked exactly as `res == FALSE` at lines 46-47, 64-65, and 79-80, routing every read failure to `corrupted`.

`bytes` (line 9, init 0) is monotone non-decreasing for non-negative `dire->size` (increments at lines 54, 69, 109), so the outer loop `while(bytes < size)` (line 44) with fixed `size` (line 42) terminates or exits via a checked read failure.
limitations: The definitions of `struct squashfs_dir_entry`, `struct squashfs_dir_header`, and `struct inode` are not in the fragment, so the signedness/width of `dire->size`, `dirh.count`, and `(*i)->data` are unknown; negative-size (lines 78, 82, 109), count-wrap (lines 51, 57), and data-underflow (line 42) claims cannot be grounded (C1/C3/C4/C6 demoted).

The exact capacity of `dire->name` cannot be pinned from the fragment: the buffer total (line 5-6) is shown, but `offsetof(struct squashfs_dir_entry, name)` is not; the off-by-one at index `dire->size + 1 == SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN` (line 82) when `dire->size == SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN-1` is therefore unconfirmable in both directions (C2).
The contract of `read_inode` (line 16) is not shown, so the NULL-dereference of `*i` (lines 24-28, 31, 40-42) has no NULL producer inside the fragment (C1).
The behavior of `read_directory_data` for a non-positive length argument (possible from line 78) is not shown, so no overflow or failure consequence is confirmable (C3).
`strdup` (line 98) can return NULL only on allocation failure, and no security-relevant operation on that failure state is visible in the fragment (C5).

No bound relating `start` (line 40) to the directory table end is shown; reads are only bounded by checked EOF failures (lines 46/64/79 -> corrupted), so this is a validation/robustness gap with no confirmed memory or injection consequence (C7).
The numeric values of `SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN` and `SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT` are not shown; the analysis treats the name-length bound and the count bound symbolically.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the fragment. The only call is rz_list_clone(qo->maps) at line 4 with no size/index/length argument derived from input and no other security-relevant sink. The unguarded dereferences of bf->o->bin_obj (line 3) and qo->maps (line 4) cannot be confirmed as NULL dereferences because the fragment contains no producer of NULL for those framework-held fields; that concern is a robustness issue, not a demonstrated vulnerability.

assumptions: Line 2 'rz_return_val_if_fail(bf && bf->o, NULL)' establishes that bf and bf->o are non-NULL on the continuation path (lines 3-4).

rz_list_clone is a standard list-cloning call whose only argument is a list pointer; its return value is returned directly to the caller and is not consumed by any security-relevant operation inside the fragment.
limitations: NULL dereference of qo (bf->o->bin_obj) at line 3 and of qo->maps at line 4 is unconfirmable: no statement in the fragment produces NULL for these framework-held fields, and framework pointers are treated as non-NULL absent a shown nullable contract; no CWE attached.
Behavior of rz_list_clone when passed a NULL list argument is not shown in the fragment, so any claim about NULL handling at line 4 depends on callee semantics outside the shown code.
No capacity, size, index, or boundary claim could be made because the fragment declares no buffers, allocations, or size computations.

verdict.summary: In the ICMPV6_PKT_TOOBIG branch, mtu = be32_to_cpu(info) - offset is computed with unsigned (u32 - int) arithmetic and only clamped on the low side (mtu < IPV6_MIN_MTU, line 68). An attacker-supplied ICMPv6 PTB can underflow it (e.g., info=0, offset=40 -> mtu=4294967256) and also set it arbitrarily high via the unconstrained u32 info field; line 70 then stores this value into t->dev->mtu with no upper-bound validation, corrupting the tunnel device's MTU/capacity and enabling MTU-poisoning/oversized-frame DoS.

evidence.reason: Sink store of an attacker-derived MTU. mtu is computed at line 67 as be32_to_cpu(info) - offset, where info (__be32, entry-point ICMPv6 PTB field) keeps its full u32 residual range and offset (int, entry-point) is unconstrained by any shown statement; usual arithmetic conversions evaluate the subtraction in u32, so info=0 with offset=40 wraps to 4294967256 (0xFFFFFFD8). The only protection, line 68's lower-bound clamp "if (mtu < IPV6_MIN_MTU) mtu = IPV6_MIN_MTU;", admits every value in [IPV6_MIN_MTU, 2^32-1], including the wrapped 4294967256, so the clamp is bypassed by unsigned underflow and the value reaches the line-70 store into t->dev->mtu (the device's packet-length capacity used by later transmit/PMTU logic), with no upper-bound validation anywhere in the fragment. Path: line 12/25 pulls admitted for a >=44-byte linear skb (attacker sets GRE flags=0, skipping lines 16/18/20), ip6gre_tunnel_lookup returns non-NULL for a matching existing tunnel (line 33 passes), and type==ICMPV6_PKT_TOOBIG selects line 66. Primary mechanism: CWE-190 unsigned underflow corrupting a security-relevant capacity value.

assumptions: ip6gre_tunnel_lookup returns non-NULL when the embedded src/dst addresses and key match a configured ip6gre tunnel, which is the normal operating condition for an ICMP error handler; the shown code handles the NULL case by returning at lines 33-34.
pskb_may_pull at lines 12/25 succeeds for attacker-crafted ICMPv6 messages that embed at least offset+grehlen linear bytes (offset=40, grehlen=4 -> 44 bytes), so the guard lines admit the witness.

type, code, and info are attacker-controlled ICMPv6 fields (entry-point inputs) with no shown constraints; offset is treated as an entry-point-derived int with full domain because the fragment never checks it.
limitations: PARAMPROB teli OOB read (lines 53-57): the guard at line 55 admits teli values up to 2^32-1 and skb->data[teli]/tel->encap_limit at lines 56-57 are read outside the line-12/25 pull window, but the skb's total/linear length is not identifiable from any declaration or allocation in the fragment, and the concrete return of the unshown ip6_tnl_parse_tlv_enc_lim cannot be simulated from shown code; per the capacity rule this is a limitation with no CWE.

Negative offset (lines 14-15, 29, 31-32): pskb_may_pull(skb, offset+4) admits offset=-4 (sum 0), allowing greh->flags reads before skb->data into headroom; caller-side provenance of offset and the skb head allocation capacity are not shown, so no confirmed OOB.

ipv6h 40-byte read (lines 27, 31-32) may extend past the pull-guaranteed offset+grehlen window when offset < 36; whether bytes are actually present depends on unshown skb->len/headlen, so unconfirmable.
be32_to_cpu(info) - 2 at line 55 wraps for info in {0,1}, but the resulting teli=0xFFFFFFFE/0xFFFFFFFF values require the unshown parser to return them, which is unconfirmed.

The PKT_TOOBIG MTU inflation may be viewed by kernel maintainers as accepted protocol behavior/robustness hardening rather than an exploitable memory-safety vulnerability; reported at low severity with confidence 0.6.

verdict.summary: SplashOutputDev::tilingPatternFill derives the tile repetition counts repeatX/repeatY directly from the unvalidated int parameters x1-x0/y1-y0 (lines 78-79 and 104-107); the only aggregate guard, `repeatX * repeatY <= 4` (line 119), is a minimum-effort filter that admits every larger product and itself overflows int. The nested loops at lines 191-197 then execute up to ~10^9-10^18 blitImage calls (sink at line 195), enabling an unbounded CPU resource-exhaustion (DoS) on a crafted pattern fill.

evidence.reason: imgData.repeatX/repeatY (lines 166-167) are set from repeatX/repeatY, whose residual range is the full int domain of the unconstrained parameters x1-x0/y1-y0 (line 4): assigned directly at lines 78-79 and via the region override at lines 104-107. The only aggregate gate, line 119 (`repeatX * repeatY <= 4`), admits every product > 4 and caps nothing, and the product itself overflows signed int. The loops at lines 191-192 therefore execute repeatX*repeatY iterations of the blitImage sink at line 195 — e.g., 32768x32768 = 2^30 calls for in-range ints, up to ~(2^31)^2 with guard overflow — an unbounded tile-repetition volume causing CPU resource exhaustion (CWE-770).

assumptions: Parameters x0,y0,x1,y1 (line 4) are not constrained anywhere in the fragment, so their residual range is the full int domain; this is what makes repeatX/repeatY (lines 78-79, 98-107) input-driven without a shown cap.
Line 119 is the only aggregate check on the repetition volume, and it is a minimum filter (rejects products <= 4) rather than a maximum.

The illustrative witness uses in-domain finite CTM/HDPI values (lines 35-40 enforce finiteness) to reach the line-70 branch; the fragment does not constrain those doubles, so the branch is reachable for a range of admitted inputs.
The else-branch while loop (lines 85-90) caps each scaled bitmap dimension at <=16384, bounding the line-127 allocation in that branch.
limitations: Signed-int overflow (UB) in repeatX * repeatY (line 119), surface_width * repeatX / surface_height * repeatY (lines 100/102), x1 - x0 (lines 50-51, 78-79, 104-107), getWidth()*repeatX (lines 170-171), and x*getWidth() (lines 193-194) is reachable for full-domain ints but only produces the same DoS class or correctness issues; no independently confirmed memory-safety sink.

Out-of-range double-to-int casts at lines 50-51, 61-62, 76-77, and 91-92 are UB for large inputs, but downstream values are mostly deflected by the area (81), zero (94), and product (119) guards; no confirmed memory corruption.

Double divisions by zero at lines 45/48 (ctm components may be finite but zero), lines 64-65, and line 72 (kx == 0 when width == 0) yield IEEE inf/NaN rather than a trap; downstream int casts are UB but no confirmed exploit path.
Non-termination of the while loop at lines 85-90 would require kx/ky to already be inf, which depends on prior UB conversions; reachability is not established.
NULL dereference after `new Splash` (line 136) and `new Gfx` (line 153) is not a finding because the shown code cannot produce a NULL from an allocation failure on any visible path.
blitImage (line 195) and drawImage (line 200) receive overflowed/negative int positions or dimensions whose effects depend on callee internals not shown in the fragment.
The area check at line 81 uses pre-scaling dimensions and an `(unsigned long)` product that can wrap on 32-bit platforms; consequences inside SplashBitmap are outside the fragment.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The guard at line 8 rejects nbytes >= MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN, leaving nbytes in [0, MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-1]; therefore memcpy at line 11 writes at most MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-1 bytes and the NUL write at line 16 lands at index <= MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-1, both inside the capacity declared at line 4 (char drc_name[MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN]). The residual concern at line 13 (strchr is called before NUL termination is guaranteed, because memcpy adds no NUL and buf's contents are unconstrained) is recorded as a limitation: any out-of-bounds extent depends on uninitialized stack values not derivable or attacker-controllable within the shown code.

assumptions: MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN is a positive named constant; per line 4, drc_name has exactly MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN elements, and the guard at line 8 uses the same constant, so the admitted range [0, MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-1] is measured against the true capacity.
nbytes is size_t (unsigned), so its domain has no negative values; the admitted set from line 8 is exactly [0, MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-1].
buf is an entry-point (sysfs store) buffer; the fragment imposes no constraint on its contents, so the copied region may contain no '\n' and no '\0'.
limitations: At line 13, strchr is called on drc_name before NUL termination is established: memcpy (line 11) adds no NUL and buf's contents within nbytes are unconstrained. For admitted input (e.g., nbytes = MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-1 bytes containing neither '\n' nor '\0'), strchr scans into the uninitialized tail (indices nbytes..MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-1); any read past the object, or any write at line 16 to a stray '\n' found past it, has indeterminate extent and depends on uninitialized stack values that no shown operation produces and the attacker does not control within the fragment. It fails the OOB confirmation standard (exact excess must be derivable from the shown code), so it carries no CWE.

If strchr finds a stale '\n' inside the uninitialized tail (in-bounds), the string passed to dlpar_add_slot (line 18) is truncated at that point; reads and writes remain in-bounds and no security impact is derivable from the fragment.
Returning 0 for over-length input at line 9 is the sysfs error convention of the surrounding mechanism; the fragment does not show the caller's interpretation, so no verdict is attached to it.
kobj and attr are unused; no trust invariants are needed for them.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. Every write to `vertices` is guarded: L30/L33 admit only `vertexIndex in [0, maxVertices-1]`, and with `groupCode` restricted to {10,20,30} (offset 0..2) or 42 (offset 3) by L22-L23/L29/L33, the maximum derived index is 4*(maxVertices-1)+3 = 4*maxVertices-1, exactly within the capacity `4*maxVertices` doubles allocated at L9. Integer-overflow, NULL-initial-state, allocation-failure, and loop-termination concerns are not confirmable because the types of `maxVertices`, `vertexIndex`, `vertices`, and the contracts of `toInt`/`toReal` are not visible in the fragment.

assumptions: Capacity of `vertices` is 4*maxVertices doubles, quoted from L9 `vertices = new double[4*maxVertices];`.
The fragment's only writer of `maxVertices` is L4, executed in the same `groupCode==90` branch whose `maxVertices>0` guard (L5) also executes the L9 allocation and resets `vertexIndex=-1` (L17).
Within L29's `groupCode<=30` sub-branch, `groupCode` is one of {10,20,30} (from L22-L23), so `groupCode/10-1` is exactly {0,1,2}; no other values reach L31.
`vertexIndex` is incremented (L26) only when L25 admits `vertexIndex < maxVertices-1`, so after increment it is at most `maxVertices-1`.
limitations: Integer overflow/wraparound in `4*maxVertices` (L9), `4*vertexIndex + (groupCode/10-1)` (L31), and `4*vertexIndex + 3` (L34) is not confirmable: the declared types of `maxVertices`/`vertexIndex` and the return type/contract of `toInt` are absent from the fragment, so the wrap cannot be shown to occur in shown types or to corrupt the allocation-size sink (CWE-190/195 candidates).

A write through a NULL `vertices` is not producible on a shown path: the write guards (L30/L33) are satisfiable only when `maxVertices>=1`, which forces the L9 allocation; a NULL state would require unshown member initialization or an unshown `new[]` failure.
Double-free/UAF via `delete[] vertices` (L7) followed by `new double[...]` (L9) requires the allocation to throw/fail, and no shown security-relevant operation runs on that failure state.

Potential non-termination of the L10 loop (`int i` compared against `maxVertices`) if `maxVertices` were an unsigned type exceeding INT_MAX cannot be assessed because its type is not shown (CWE-835 candidate).
The initial values of `vertices`, `vertexIndex`, and `maxVertices` are not shown; any finding depending on a stale/inconsistent initial state is out of scope for this fragment.

verdict.summary: squashfs_opendir validates only the upper bound of the image-controlled directory-entry size at line 85, so negative values of dire->size (e.g. -14) pass the guard and drive an out-of-bounds stack write at line 96 (dire->name[-13] = '\0' lands one byte below the stack buffer declared at line 5) as well as a negative length into read_directory_data at lines 90-91. A crafted squashfs image can corrupt the stack (CWE-787).

evidence.reason: Image-controlled dire->size (read at lines 71-77, residual range [-32768, SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN-1]) is the only size constraint, line 85, which excludes only values >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN and admits negatives. For size = -14 the subscript dire->size + 1 = -13 writes buffer + offsetof(dire->name) - 13 = one byte below the stack buffer declared at line 5 (char buffer[sizeof(squashfs_dir_entry_3) + SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1], name tail capacity 257); size = -32768 writes 32755 bytes below. Witness passes every guard on the path: line 54 (header read ok), line 63 (dir_count=1 <= SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT), line 79 (entry read ok), line 85 (-14 < SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN). Primary CWE-787: out-of-bounds stack write via an input-derived index.

The length argument dire->size + 1 is derived from the same image value that passes the upper-only guard at line 85; for any negative residual value (e.g. -14 yields length -13) the argument is negative, which is outside the domain of a read-length parameter and cannot be proven in-domain for the whole admitted set. This is the call-site component of the same CWE-787 finding: the shown code derives an out-of-domain length, and a no-op-success read (index < length semantics) lets the write at line 96 execute below the buffer.

assumptions: The capacity of the destination object is visible at line 5: char buffer[sizeof(squashfs_dir_entry_3) + SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1], with dire = buffer at line 7, so the fixed entry part is sizeof(squashfs_dir_entry_3) bytes and the name tail has SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1 bytes.

Line 85 is the only fragment-visible constraint on dire->size and it bound only the upper side (rejecting values >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN); the fragment contains no lower-bound check between lines 71-77 and 96.
The negative-write claim does not depend on the numeric values of the named constants SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN / SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT, only on the guard semantics visible at lines 63 and 85.
limitations: The struct squashfs_dir_entry_3 definition is not in the fragment; the analysis assumes the standard squashfs layout (signed 16-bit short size field, trailing char name[] starting at offset sizeof(squashfs_dir_entry_3) = 12). If dire->size were an unsigned type, the negative-size path would be unreachable and this finding would not hold; the fragment does not show the declaration, which caps confidence at 0.7.

The behavior of read_directory_data for a negative length is not visible; if it returns FALSE for negative lengths, the line-96 write is skipped, but the negative length argument at lines 90-91 remains a confirmed out-of-domain call-site derivation either way.

read_inode's return at line 17 is never NULL-checked before *i is dereferenced at lines 25-29/32/41-43; a NULL producer is not visible in the fragment, so the NULL-dereference candidate is unconfirmed.

The corrupted: path (lines 129-130) ends the fragment without a return expression (falling off the end of a non-void function is UB); this is likely an artifact of fragment truncation and its caller-side impact is not shown, so it is not reported.

Integer conversion at line 43 (size = (*i)->data + bytes - 3, unsigned to int) can yield a negative size and skip the loop, and negative-size entries can shrink bytes (line 123); no confirmed memory sink results and the outer loop terminates via metadata exhaustion, so no integer-overflow or CWE-835 finding is reported.

strdup/TRACE reading an underfilled dire->name for negative sizes (own stack-buffer over-read) depends on uninitialized stack contents and is a secondary effect of the primary write; not reported as an independent CWE.

verdict.summary: In udf_expand_file_adinicb, the on-disk-derived length iinfo->i_lenAlloc is only checked for non-zero (line 9) before it is used as both an offset and a length. At lines 32-33 the expression PAGE_SIZE - iinfo->i_lenAlloc underflows for i_lenAlloc > PAGE_SIZE (e.g., 4097 on 4K pages), producing an ~2^64-byte memset from kaddr+4097 against a PAGE_SIZE-byte page-cache page, and at lines 34-35 memcpy writes i_lenAlloc bytes into the same 4096-byte page. Both are kernel heap out-of-bounds writes (CWE-787) caused by the unchecked arithmetic (CWE-190).

evidence.reason: iinfo->i_lenAlloc retains the full non-zero loff_t domain (line 9 excludes only 0; no other shown statement bounds it). It drives both the offset kaddr + i_lenAlloc and the length PAGE_SIZE - i_lenAlloc. For the admitted witness i_lenAlloc = 4097: offset = kaddr+4097 (1 byte past the page, whose 4096-byte capacity is fixed by this same expression's use of PAGE_SIZE), and PAGE_SIZE - i_lenAlloc = -1 wraps to 2^64-1 in unsigned long arithmetic (line 33), so memset performs an out-of-bounds heap write of ~2^64 bytes. Primary CWE-787 (OOB write via attacker-influenced index/size); the wrap of the size argument is the independent CWE-190 root cause.

The same unvalidated iinfo->i_lenAlloc (residual range: any non-zero loff_t; only the line-9 truthiness check precedes it) is passed as the byte count to memcpy, whose destination kaddr is a 4096-byte page (capacity PAGE_SIZE, established by the line 32-33 page-remainder arithmetic). With the admitted witness i_lenAlloc = 4097, memcpy writes 4097 bytes into the 4096-byte page, a 1-byte heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787); larger admitted values overflow further. The source-side read from iinfo->i_data is not counted because i_data's capacity is not shown in the fragment.

assumptions: kaddr = kmap_atomic(page) (line 31) with page from find_or_create_page(inode->i_mapping, 0, GFP_NOFS) (line 26) maps a PAGE_SIZE-byte buffer; the fragment itself asserts this capacity at line 33 by computing the remaining page space as PAGE_SIZE - iinfo->i_lenAlloc.

iinfo->i_lenAlloc and iinfo->i_lenEAttr are 64-bit loff_t fields per the UDF inode layout, though their declarations are outside the fragment. The confirmed witness (i_lenAlloc = PAGE_SIZE+1) is valid under C usual arithmetic regardless of the signedness assumption: PAGE_SIZE is unsigned long, and 4096 - 4097 wraps to 2^64-1 in the unsigned result type.
A freshly returned page from find_or_create_page at index 0 is not PageUptodate, so the branch at line 30 is reachable; nothing in the fragment marks the page uptodate before line 37.
limitations: memset(iinfo->i_data + iinfo->i_lenEAttr, 0x00, iinfo->i_lenAlloc) (lines 41-42), the write side of memcpy at line 59, and the read side of memcpy at lines 34-35 into iinfo->i_data are not confirmed as OOB because iinfo->i_data has no declaration/allocation/named capacity in the shown fragment.

verdict.summary: add_slot_store copies attacker-controlled buf into the fixed MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN stack array drc_name via strscpy(drc_name, buf, nbytes + 1) and discards the return value. Because the fragment never establishes a NUL byte in buf, an admitted input (nbytes = MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-1 with all-non-NUL bytes) can leave drc_name unterminated, and the subsequent strchr(drc_name, '\n') at line 13 (and dlpar_add_slot(drc_name) at line 17) scan past the end of the stack array: a stack out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) enabled by unchecked strscpy status / improper NUL termination.

evidence.reason: Sink: strchr scans drc_name as a NUL-terminated string. Source: buf (entry-point input, unconstrained content, no shown NUL guarantee) and nbytes (residual [0, MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-1] per the guard at line 8) flow into strscpy at line 11 with count nbytes+1; for witness nbytes = MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-1 and 256 non-NUL bytes, strscpy fills drc_name[MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN] (capacity declared at line 4) exactly and returns -E2BIG without a terminator, which is discarded. strchr then reads index MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN, one past the array's last valid index MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-1 — stack OOB read (CWE-125) with excess of at least one byte.

Second sink: drc_name is passed to dlpar_add_slot as a C string while it may be a non-NUL-terminated stack buffer (same witness as above: 256 non-NUL bytes copied at line 11, length argument nbytes+1 derived from the admitted input, status discarded). The callee's string consumption reads past the MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-byte array declared at line 4 — the same stack OOB read (CWE-125), anchored at this call site.

assumptions: MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN is the same positive compile-time constant in the declaration at line 4 (array size, valid indices 0..MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-1) and the comparison at line 8.
nbytes (store-handler length parameter) denotes the number of written data bytes available at buf; the fragment's use of nbytes as the copy length and its guard at line 8 rely on that role.

strscpy(dst, src, count) at line 11 follows the standard contract: it writes at most count bytes and appends a NUL terminator only if a NUL is read from the source within the copy window, otherwise it writes count bytes and returns -E2BIG without terminating dst.
limitations: The finding rests on the residual range of buf's content — specifically the absence of a NUL byte within the copy window. The byte at buf[nbytes] (the (nbytes+1)-th byte read by strscpy) lies beyond the nbytes attacker-written bytes and is not shown; a framework-provided NUL terminator there (an invariant not visible in the fragment) would prevent the OOB read. This is why confidence is capped at 0.6.

A potential one-byte stack OOB write at line 15 (*end = '\0') would additionally require strchr to locate a '\n' beyond the array, which depends on uninitialized stack contents not shown in the fragment; not separately confirmed.
dlpar_add_slot's body is not shown; its OOB read is anchored only on standard C-string parameter semantics implied by its name and by the passing of drc_name.
Reachability by an unprivileged attacker depends on sysfs file permissions, which are not visible in the fragment.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds read in SetGrayscaleImage: for a PseudoClass image, colormap_index is allocated with image->colors+1 entries (line 26-27), but the pixel-remap loop indexes it with ScaleQuantumToMap(GetPixelIndex(image,q)) (lines 148-149). The stored pixel index is entry-point image data with no visible bound in the fragment; a pixel index that maps to >= colors+1 reads past the end of the colormap_index buffer (e.g., colors=1 with pixel index mapping to 2 reads 8 bytes at offset 16 of a 16-byte allocation). The non-PseudoClass branch is protected by the MaxColormapSize+1 allocation (lines 29-30), which does not apply to the PseudoClass path, and no guard between line 26 and line 149 clamps the index.

evidence.reason: CWE-125 heap OOB read: the subscript arg is ScaleQuantumToMap(GetPixelIndex(image,q)); GetPixelIndex returns the stored pixel index quantum, an entry-point (image-data) value that no shown statement constrains, so its residual range is the full Quantum domain. The capacity of colormap_index on the PseudoClass path is image->colors+1 elements (AcquireQuantumMemory(image->colors+1, sizeof(*colormap_index)), lines 26-27). Witness: PseudoClass image with image->colors=1 (2-element buffer) and one pixel whose stored index maps to 2 (identity scaling in default 16-bit configuration; code's own model puts scale outputs up to MaxColormapSize) -> index == capacity -> reads 8 bytes (one ssize_t element) past the end. Guards on the path (lines 138, 141; loops at 130 and 146) all pass and never bound the index; the protective MaxColormapSize+1 sizing (lines 29-30) applies only to the non-PseudoClass branch. The OOB value is then stored as the pixel index by SetPixelIndex.

assumptions: ScaleQuantumToMap maps the full Quantum domain into the colormap-map domain whose extent the code itself sizes as MaxColormapSize+1 entries (lines 29-30); in default 16-bit builds QuantumRange==MaxMap makes it the identity for small indices.
Pixel index quanta of a PseudoClass image are externally supplied image data (entry-point); the fragment contains no constraint on them.
AcquireQuantumMemory failure is handled by ThrowBinaryException (lines 31-33, 104-109), which returns MagickFalse.
limitations: The exact numeric excess beyond colors+1 depends on invisible constants MaxMap/QuantumRange/MaxColormapSize, not declared in the fragment; the finding rests on the code's own allocation model, so confidence is capped at 0.7.

colormap[j]=image->colormap[0] (line 111) with image->colors==0 would be an OOB write/read, but requires zero-color/zero-pixel images and an AcquireQuantumMemory(0) result that is non-NULL — neither is established by the fragment.

First-block indexing colormap_index[intensity] and image->colormap[image->colors] (lines 74, 81-88) is in-bounds only if ScaleQuantumToMap output < MaxColormapSize; the numeric value is invisible, so this boundary is unconfirmable in either direction.

The discarded return of TransformImageColorspace (line 24) is an error-status-handling concern (CWE-754/703 candidate) but no security-relevant operation in the fragment runs on the failed-conversion state, so it has no confirmed impact.
AcquireAuthenticCacheView returns (lines 46, 125) are unchecked; treated as non-NULL per analysis rules since no nullable contract is visible in the fragment.

All remaining branches (ESC guard line 39, aborting() line 46, new_cmdpos clamp lines 55-62) are internally consistent, and there are no loops or injection/crypto/file sinks.

Any memory-safety claim about ccline.cmdpos/ccline.cmdlen and the command-line buffer requires the capacity of ccline.cmdbuff, which is not visible in the fragment (no CWE).

This not-vulnerable verdict is a default verdict: no sink, capacity, or decisive protective statement is available inside the fragment, so confidence is capped at 0.7 by the calibration rules and set to 0.6.

verdict.summary: Signed integer overflow in tilingPatternFill: attacker-controlled repeatX = x1 - x0 (lines 78/101, passed to imgData at line 162) times the tile bitmap width overflows int at line 166, and the tile-loop index x * tBitmap->getWidth() overflows at line 189; the wrapped values are consumed as tile sizes/coordinates by splash->drawImage (line 196) and splash->blitImage (line 191), i.e., a confirmed CWE-190 corrupting sizes/indexes for memory-consuming rasterization.

evidence.reason: result_width is declared int (line 12). repeatX is an untrusted int set directly from x1 - x0 at lines 78/101 (entry-point params with no shown constraint, full int domain), copied to imgData.repeatX at line 162. getWidth() returns the SplashBitmap width created at lines 123-124 from surface_width. Witness: surface_width = 36, repeatX = 60,000,000 -> 36 * 60,000,000 = 2,160,000,000 > INT_MAX (2,147,483,647), an overflow (CWE-190) wrapping to -2,134,967,296, which is then consumed at line 196 as the width argument of splash->drawImage (a size parameter by name and use). Line 115 admits the witness (product = 1,200,000,000 > 4, no upper cap; dims nonzero); lines 125 guards do not trigger.

Loop bound imgData.repeatX (line 188) is the attacker int from line 78/162; tBitmap->getWidth() = 36 from the line 123-124 allocation. For the admitted guard set (line 115 passes, e.g. repeatX = 1,000,000,000, repeatY = 20 -> product 2e9 > 4), x progresses to 1e9-1 and x * 36 wraps for every x >= 59,652,324 (36*59,652,324 = 2,147,483,664 > INT_MAX). The wrapped x0 (int, line 4) is passed to splash->blitImage at line 191 as a destination coordinate (index parameter), a second CWE-190 instance of the same root cause (unbounded repeat count from x1 - x0).

assumptions: HDPI = VDPI = 144 (lines 52-53) so kx = ky = 2; any positive DPI works for the witness.
ptm[0] = ptm[3] = 1 and mat = (0.9, 0, 0, 0.05, 0, 0) with a diagonal page CTM realize the witness values; these are entry-point PDF matrix inputs with no in-fragment constraint.

SplashBitmap::getWidth()/getHeight() return int (assigned to int and multiplied with the int repeatX at line 166; the constructor width/height arguments at lines 123-124 are the visible capacity source).

The tile bitmap capacity visible in the fragment is surface_width x surface_height (lines 123-124), i.e., 36 x 2 = 72 pixels (mono8) for the witness.
limitations: An actual out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) at blitImage (line 191) / drawImage (line 196) cannot be confirmed because the destination surface (formerSplash/bitmap) capacity is not visible in the fragment.

Division-by-zero producing NaN (lines 45, 48, 64-65, 72) and subsequent (int)ceil(NaN/inf) conversions (lines 50-51, 61-62, 76-77, 91-92) are UB with implementation-defined values; no concrete downstream consequence can be proven from the fragment, so these are not reported as findings.
Line 81 (unsigned long) surface_width * surface_height can wrap only on 32-bit unsigned long (platform-dependent), and the line 85-90 halving loop caps the final tile size; not reported.
The guard at line 115 (repeatX * repeatY <= 4) itself overflows for large repeat products (signed-overflow UB); the witness avoids that overflow, so this is not a confirmed finding.

The tile loops (lines 187-193) admit up to ~2^31 blitImage calls (guard is only a lower bound), a potential DoS (CWE-770/CWE-400) but the same repeatX flow as the confirmed CWE-190, so not an independent finding.
gfx->display(str) (line 153) parses PDF content outside the fragment; content-parser vulnerabilities are out of scope.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable within the fragment. The only guard (`if (!block)` at L3) restricts `block` to non-NULL, and its consumers (L11, L16) both require non-NULL, so the in-fragment path is in-domain for every shown sink. limitations: Use-after-free via missing RCU grace period (CWE-416 unconfirmed): `QLIST_REMOVE_RCU(block, next)` at L11 followed immediately by `reclaim_ramblock(uc, block)` at L16, with the deferred `call_rcu` path commented at L15, frees a node while a concurrent reader of `uc->ram_list.blocks` could still dereference it. The claim fails Part 2 because the dereferencing reader exists only outside the fragment.

Double-free (CWE-415 unconfirmed) if `qemu_ram_free` is invoked twice on the same `block`: L11 and L16 would operate on freed storage. No in-fragment path performs a second invocation; it is caller-dependent.

NULL-pointer dereference of `uc` at L12 (CWE-476 unconfirmed) if the caller passes NULL: L3 guards only `block`, but a NULL `uc` cannot be produced by any statement in the fragment, so it is out-of-scope.
Safety of freeing `block` while other RAMBlocks or caches besides `uc->ram_list.mru_block` (cleared at L12) alias its storage depends on caller invariants not shown in the fragment.

verdict.summary: The signed int width parameters (left_width, src_width, right_width) are passed unvalidated as memcpy length arguments. It is implicitly converted to size_t as the memcpy length: left_width=-1 yields length SIZE_MAX, unreadable/unwritable by any finite object, producing an unbounded OOB read from src_strip+left_offset and OOB write to dest_strip (CWE-195).

src_width is unvalidated int; the only guard on the path (for (ii = 0; ii < num_tiles; ii++), line 12) constrains only the iteration count, not src_width. With num_tiles=1 and src_width=-1, the body executes (ii=0 admitted) and passes SIZE_MAX as the memcpy length, causing an unbounded OOB write to ptr_out_temp/dest_strip and OOB read from src_strip (CWE-195).

All parameter widths are unconstrained: the fragment contains no check, clamp, or minimum/maximum on left_width, src_width, right_width, left_offset, or num_tiles.
limitations: The capacities of dest_strip and src_strip are not declared or derivable in the fragment, so the magnitude of the resulting OOB read/write cannot be quantified and CWE-787/CWE-125 cannot be independently confirmed as primary or secondary.
A negative left_offset at line 9 produces an OOB read before src_strip, but the source object's bounds are not identifiable, so it is not reported as a finding.

The #ifdef PACIFY_VALGRIND block (lines 18-23) is gated by a macro whose state is not shown and uses LAND_BITS, which is undefined in the fragment; its activation and behavior (including the pointer-difference UB at line 20) are unconfirmable.

Caller provenance of irq/irq_flags and whether the interrupt layer can invoke this function in contexts where get_irq_regs() returns NULL are out of scope for the fragment; that external condition is exactly why the NULL-regs flow was recorded as a limitation rather than a confirmed deref.

NULL is out of domain for the "%s" argument, causing undefined behavior / NULL dereference inside the formatter (CWE-476), same root cause as line 134.

On the same non-empty-image path (guard 133 false), the unvalidated NULL arg1 is forwarded as the filename argument to WriteImages; the fragment derives this NULL at line 26 from entry-point arg1n (admitted NULL per lines 23-24/34) with no intervening constraint, so the filename parameter receives an out-of-domain NULL pointer (CWE-476).

`_images == NULL` is an expected state because the fragment explicitly tests it at line 133 (and 158, 181) and the write-branch comment at 132-133 calls the empty-list case a supported path.
LocaleCompare, FormatLocaleString, and WriteImages consume C strings per their standard name-implied contracts (non-NULL); their bodies are not shown in the fragment.
The `key` buffer capacity is the constant MagickPathExtent (line 124), but its numeric value is not visible, so no overrun claim is made for the bounded FormatLocaleString call.

The NULL-dereference at line 134 assumes `LocaleCompare` itself does not tolerate NULL (its implementation is outside the fragment); if it is NULL-tolerant the crash does not occur, though the call site is still out of domain for a standard string compare.
Results of PingImages/ReadImages (108/110) are not NULL-checked before AppendImageToList (111); read-failure semantics are callee-side and unconfirmed.

Results of CloneImageList/CloneImageInfo (141-142) are not NULL-checked before WriteImages (143); this is a plain OOM path without attacker-controlled volume shown, so it is not a confirmed error-handling finding.

The asserts at lines 16-18 rely on caller-provided wand validity and are not attacker-input driven.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in SetGrayscaleImage at line 111: colormap is allocated with image->colors elements at line 103, and when image->colors == 0 (reachable for a DirectClass image with rows==0/columns==0, or a PseudoClass image with an empty colormap) the object has 0 bytes, yet line 111 writes colormap[0] = image->colormap[0], a full PixelInfo record past the zero-byte allocation whenever the 0-size allocation returns non-NULL. The only guard (lines 104-109) excludes only the NULL outcome. Lines 121-123 then leave image->colors=1 with a 0-element colormap, feeding inconsistent state to later consumers such as SetImageMonochrome (line 158).

evidence.reason: Capacity grounding: line 103 allocates colormap with count = image->colors (0 bytes when image->colors==0), and image->colors is explicitly reset to 0 at line 44 with no shown statement establishing a minimum (Phase 1 residual range includes 0; the row/column loops at lines 51 and 68 simply skip for zero dimensions). The guard at lines 104-109 admits every non-NULL outcome, including a non-NULL pointer to a 0-byte allocation from malloc(0)-style behavior, so it does not protect the sink; the OOB write is reachable on the shown path (DirectClass image, rows==0, columns==0: lines 38→44→103→111 with checks at 31/38/104 all passed). assumptions: MagickMax(a,b) (lines 26-30) returns the larger operand, so the non-PseudoClass colormap_index allocation has at least MaxColormapSize+1 elements, keeping the MaxColormapSize-element memset at lines 36-37 in bounds without needing the numeric value of either constant.
The asserts at lines 21-22 establish a non-NULL image (debug builds); analysis treats image as non-NULL.
AcquireImageColormap (line 38) returning MagickTrue is taken to provide a non-NULL image->colormap with MaxColormapSize entries; on failure lines 40-42 abort the function.
qsort with nmemb==0 (reached when image->colors==0) performs no comparisons and is treated as a no-op per the C standard.
limitations: Index-domain claims for colormap_index[intensity] (lines 74/79/81/91) and colormap_index[ScaleQuantumToMap(GetPixelIndex(...))] (lines 148-149) are unconfirmable: the numeric values of MaxMap and MaxColormapSize and the output bound of ScaleQuantumToMap are not visible in the fragment.

Whether image->colors can outgrow the MaxColormapSize-entry colormap in the first pass (lines 82-88) cannot be bounded without the distinct-intensity domain (ScaleQuantumToMap/MaxMap), so a colormap overflow there is unconfirmed.

The confirmed out-of-bounds write at line 111 depends on a 0-size allocation returning non-NULL; if it returns NULL, lines 104-109 throw and no write occurs. The write itself is out of bounds under the C standard in either non-NULL case.

The discarded return of TransformImageColorspace (lines 23-24) and the unconditional status overwrite at line 124 (which clobbers first-pass failures recorded at lines 65/95) are error-handling weaknesses with no direct security-relevant sink inside the fragment.

A PseudoClass empty-colormap variant of the line 111 issue would additionally read image->colormap[0] from a possibly NULL old colormap; whether a PseudoClass image may have colors==0 with a NULL colormap is a reader invariant not shown, so the DirectClass zero-pixel witness is the primary demonstration.

The unshown return(status) would be the only uninitialized use of status on the PseudoClass path, but line 124 initializes status before every shown read, so no uninitialized-use finding is made within the shown code.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read in networkstatus_parse_vote_from_string: the guard `if (tok->n_args > 1)` (line 42) admits n_args == 2, but the unknown-flavor error branch then reads `tok->args[2]` (line 46), which is outside the valid range [0, n_args) established by the fragment's own indexing convention (e.g., lines 122, 203). An attacker-controlled vote/consensus header line like `network-status-version 3 not-a-flavor` reaches the sink and the stray/uninitialized pointer is consumed by escaped(), causing a heap OOB read or wild-pointer dereference (CWE-125) and a remote crash.

verdict.summary: Confirmed heap buffer overflow (CWE-787) in the xml:lang emission block: line 113 allocates buf_length+1 bytes, but line 121 passes buf_length = XML_LANG_PREFIX_LEN+lang_len+1 as the escape capacity, which exceeds the bytes actually available after the 10-byte 'xml:lang="' prefix (line 117) and the 2-byte quote/NUL tail (lines 122-123); an xml_language with escapable characters (e.g. five '&') makes raptor_xml_escape_string write past the allocation and the unconditional tail writes overflow further. Independently confirmed out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) at line 53: the namespace-dedup loop indexes element->attributes[j] with j up to nspace_declarations_count-1, which exceeds attribute_count once the element namespace and earlier attribute namespaces are recorded (witness: attribute_count=2, out-of-scope element namespace, two distinct out-of-scope attribute namespaces).

evidence.reason: CWE-787 heap overflow: buflen argument is derived at line 112 as buf_length = 10 + lang_len + 1, but the destination region for the escape output has only lang_len usable bytes: allocation is buf_length+1 bytes (line 113), the 10-byte prefix is consumed at line 117 and the quote/NUL tail (lines 122-123) needs 2 more. The passed capacity exceeds the safe escape space by 11 bytes (9 over the raw remaining region), so a callee honoring its stated capacity writes out of bounds. Witness: lang_len=5, xml_language="&&&&&", needing 25 escaped bytes; writes up to buf_length=16 bytes at indices 10..25 exceed the allocation's last valid index 10+lang_len+1=16 (line 113's capacity), and the input content is unconstrained beyond the non-NULL check at line 109.

Same CWE-787 root cause: the tail writes at p+written are unconditional. For any escape output longer than lang_len (any xml_language containing escapable characters, e.g. lang_len=5 of '&' yielding written >= 8), the quote and NUL land beyond the last valid index 10+lang_len+1 defined by the allocation at line 113, extending the heap OOB write by up to 2 more bytes.

CWE-125 out-of-bounds read: j is admitted by the guard at line 52 as j in [0, nspace_declarations_count), and count is grown at lines 36/65/77 to 1+2i by i-th iteration. With attribute_count=2, element name namespace N0 declared (line 36, count=1), and two distinct out-of-scope attribute namespaces A0,A1 (admitted by guards at lines 43 and 45-46), iteration i=1 starts with count=3; j=2 then reads element->attributes[2], which is index == capacity of the 2-element attributes array (capacity = attribute_count, per the fragment's own indexing at lines 41/43/46/61/72), and dereferences the out-of-bounds pointer. No statement in the fragment bounds nspace_declarations_count by attribute_count.

assumptions: element->attributes holds exactly element->attribute_count entries; the fragment indexes attributes[i] only for i < attribute_count (lines 41, 43, 46, 61, 72).
raptor_namespaces_namespace_in_scope returns false for the witness namespaces, which the branch at line 45-46 explicitly admits.
raptor_xml_escape_string's buflen parameter is a destination capacity consumed as such (name and call-site use); the flaw is the caller-derived oversized argument.
nspace_declarations array capacity arithmetic (lines 14-20) exactly covers the maximum appends: 1 element-ns + 2*attribute_count + declared_nspaces size + 1 xml:lang entry.
limitations: Signed overflow in element->attribute_count * 2 (line 14) would require attribute_count >= 2^30 and a matching attributes array; no concrete usable witness, demoted.

Negative attribute_count or a negative raptor_sequence_size (line 18) could drive the unsigned loop bounds at lines 41/84 into non-termination or OOB, but the fragment nowhere establishes negativity; unconfirmable.
Unchecked RAPTOR_MALLOC at line 113 followed by memcpy at line 117 is a NULL-deref only on OOM (potential CWE-476); single-shot with no attacker-controlled trigger, recorded as robustness concern.

If the real callee stopped writing far below its stated capacity (written < 8 for five '&'), the escape call itself would not overflow; the caller-side oversized-capacity derivation and the unguarded tail writes remain the confirmed flaw for any written >= lang_len+1.

verdict.summary: Integer overflow in `outlen = data_len + EVP_CIPHER_block_size(cipher_type)` (line 46): entry-point `data_len` is parsed at line 14 with residual range [0, INT_MAX] and no shown length cap, so adding the positive block size wraps the signed int. The wrapped value is consumed at line 47 as the allocation size by `emalloc(outlen + 1)` (negative int widened to a huge size_t), forcing allocation failure and a Zend fatal error (request/process termination). All intervening guards (lines 18, 24, 29) admit the witness (e.g., data_len=2147483647, method="aes-256-cbc", raw_input=true); no overflow check exists between parse and sink.

Line 46 computes `outlen = data_len + EVP_CIPHER_block_size(cipher_type)` in signed int; for data_len=2147483647 and block size 16 the sum wraps to -2147483633, and `outlen + 1 = -2147483632` is widened to size_t 0xFFFFFFFF80000010 at this call, so emalloc fails and Zend raises a fatal error (DoS). Every guard on the path admits the witness: line 18 (method_len=11), line 24 (valid cipher), line 29 (raw_input=true skips decode, so data_len keeps full parsed range); no statement in the fragment caps or checks data_len/outlen, and the absent check is the required overflow guard. The write never reaches line 54 because this allocation fails first.

assumptions: zend_parse_parameters with "s" yields non-negative int lengths in [0, INT_MAX] for data_len/password_len (no shown cap in the fragment).

EVP_CIPHER_block_size returns a positive int (>= 1) for ciphers admitted by the line 24 check (OpenSSL contract; e.g., 16 for AES-CBC); only positivity is relied on, since data_len=INT_MAX wraps for any b >= 1.
emalloc failure terminates the request/process via a Zend fatal error (Zend MM contract; the fragment does not handle allocation failure).

EVP_DecryptUpdate plus EVP_DecryptFinal total output does not exceed data_len + block_size (OpenSSL output-bound contract), which keeps the line 54 and line 58 writes in-bounds; this bound is not stated in the fragment.

EVP_CIPHER_CTX_set_key_length(&cipher_ctx, password_len) at line 51 is called with unbounded entry-point password_len and its return status is discarded; whether the callee validates or writes out-of-domain is not determinable from shown code (modern OpenSSL returns failure for fixed-key-length ciphers).

Discarded return values of EVP_DecryptInit/EVP_DecryptInit_ex/EVP_DecryptUpdate (lines 49, 53, 54) combined with uninitialized `i` (line 8) could only matter if an init failure were followed by a successful DecryptFinal — a chain no shown statement produces.
The NUL write at line 58 and the EVP_DecryptUpdate write at line 54 are judged in-bounds only under the OpenSSL output-bound contract stated in assumptions; it is not rendered in the fragment.

No heap buffer overflow via a small wrapped buffer is reachable: for every data_len in [0, INT_MAX] where the line 46 addition wraps, outlen is negative, so the emalloc argument is always a huge size_t and the allocation fails before any write.
php_openssl_validate_iv internals (reallocating/freeing iv) are not visible; free_iv-gated efree at line 68 is taken at face value.

verdict.summary: No confirmed security vulnerability. The only security-relevant sink, snprintf at line 22, is bounded by sizeof(sd->name) at the same call site, and no shown input is attacker-controlled or reaches a sink with an input-derived size or index. The two error-handling concerns (state leak when kfifo_alloc fails at lines 13-14; discarded v4l2_subdev_call statuses at lines 36 and 40) are demoted: the leak is single-shot and non-compounding, and the discarded statuses have no demonstrated security-relevant operation running on the failure state.

The probe parameter dev is framework-provided; no statement in the fragment marks it nullable, so NULL for dev is not producible inside the fragment.
