cp->rawsize is nonzero after the line 81 rejection (it is not modified before the division at line 405).
cp->tilewidth and cp->tileheight are nonzero before JPC_CEILDIV (lines 313-316) because lines 291-300 exit on zero.
limitations: C1 (highest concern): maxrlvls from line 166 drives the write loop at lines 282-285 with no upper-bound check in the fragment (line 376 only requires >= 1 and executes after the loop). OOB write into prcwidthexpns/prcheightexpns cannot be confirmed because the array capacities are not declared in the fragment; non-termination for maxrlvls > 65535 additionally depends on uint_fast16_t being 16-bit, which the fragment does not establish.

C2: cp->numtiles = numhtiles * numvtiles (line 317) can wrap uint_fast32_t for large tile counts, but no shown statement consumes numtiles in a security-relevant operation (allocation, index, length, loop bound); storage into the struct alone is not a confirmed finding.

C3: the wrapping chain hsteplcm/vsteplcm (lines 59-60), imgareatlx/imgareatly *= (lines 234, 242), refgrdwidth/refgrdheight (lines 244-245), default tilewidth/tileheight subtractions (lines 253, 256), and the tile-grid guard (lines 303-306) all use unsigned arithmetic that can wrap and admit corrupted geometry; their results only reach stored fields (numhtiles/numvtiles/numtiles) within the fragment.

C4: the ilyrrates copy at lines 325-327 writes exactly the allocated element count (numlyrs-1, lines 321-322), but the read of ilyrrates[i] is safe only under jpc_atoaf's unshown sizing contract (that it allocates exactly *numilyrrates doubles); the callee body is not in the fragment.

C5: jas_tvparser_next's return (line 106) is discarded after the loop; if a nonzero return can denote a parse error rather than EOF, partially parsed options proceed, but the callee's error semantics and any concrete security consequence are not shown in the fragment.
C6: atoi(-1) stored into uint_fast32_t fields collides with the UINT_FAST32_MAX 'unset' sentinel (lines 113, 228-229) and is reset to 0; no security impact is demonstrated within the fragment.
C7: JPC_POW2 of a negative cblkwidthexpn/cblkheightexpn (lines 352, 359) is reachable on the error path, but the macro definition is not shown.

C8: option values reach jas_eprintf as raw %s arguments (lines 147-148, 156-157, 205-206, 214-215) so control characters survive, but the sink is a stderr diagnostics channel and the fragment never establishes it as a security log (CWE-117 unconfirmed).

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The only attacker-influenced values reaching a fixed buffer are bounded by visible capacities: bv[2*MAXVALLEN] (line 22) with a sizeof(bv)-1 (line 122) destination cap that exactly accommodates the two bytes appended at lines 124-125, and snprintf into b[12] (lines 20, 91). The remaining suspicious spots (decodearr into lfparr[8], the nextvar loop, strlen on value) depend on unshown callee contracts and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: Buffer capacities are visible in the fragment: lfparr[8] (line 19), b[12] (line 20), bn[2*MAXVARLEN] (line 21), bv[2*MAXVALLEN] (line 22).
The switch at lines 34-115 enumerates the varfmt result domain visible in the fragment, making the default arm (110-114) unreachable without a varfmt contract breach.
The literal-format fprintf calls (lines 26-28, 111-112) and output() consume strings as data, so dump of arbitrary text is possible only as it already exists; no format-string injection is derivable.
limitations: atoascii's contract (destsize includes the terminating NUL) is not shown in the fragment; the append at lines 124-125 is exactly in-bounds under that standard semantics, and remains in-bounds under a data-byte-count reading for any MAXVALLEN >= 2, but a 1-byte overflow at bv[len+1] (line 125) would require both a non-standard callee and MAXVALLEN <= 1, neither derivable from the shown code.

decodearr(value, &narr, lfparr) at line 97 can write into the 8-element lfparr (line 19) and outputarr (line 100) reads narr elements; whether the callee bounds narr <= 8 is not visible or name-implied, so an OOB read/write there is unconfirmable (no CWE).

The while (nextvar(&length, &data, &name, &value)) loop at line 31: termination, pointer advance, and length handling are entirely inside the callee; non-termination (CWE-835) or parser OOB cannot be confirmed from the fragment.
strlen(value) at line 65 and strlen(bv) at line 123 assume NUL-terminated name/value; termination is a nextvar contract not visible in the fragment, so an unbounded read is unconfirmable.

The default-case fprintf at lines 111-112 with attacker-influenced name/value would at most be a stderr diagnostic (log-injection candidate); reachability requires varfmt (line 32) to return a value outside the shown case set, which is not demonstrated.
snprintf at line 91 silently truncates large octal values of uval into b[12] (line 20); truncation has no security impact.
MAXVARLEN/MAXVALLEN values are not shown; all derived bounds above are relative (2*MAXVALLEN vs MAXVALLEN) and hold for any MAXVALLEN >= 2 under standard sanitizer semantics.

verdict.summary: Two low-severity issues confirmed in the shown code: (1) the extraction write `out << *in;` (line 57) discards the stream's error status — the only probe, `out.failedToOpen()` (line 54), covers open-time failures only — so a partial/failed write still reaches `return Result::ok();` (line 64) and truncated extraction is silently reported as success (CWE-754); (2) the symlink branch reads the entire attacker-controlled entry payload into memory with no size cap via `in->readEntireStreamAsString()` (lines 44-45), enabling memory-exhaustion DoS (CWE-400). The containment guard `isAChildOf` (line 16), the symlink-part gate (line 36), and the null/open/delete/create checks are present; path-traversal, unchecked-index OOB, and cross-invocation symlink write-through claims are unconfirmable from this fragment.

evidence.reason: CWE-754: the sink write at line 57 discards the FileOutputStream error status; the only shown write-related probe is `if (out.failedToOpen())` at line 54, which checks only open success and does not cover a mid-stream failure (e.g., disk full) of the subsequent copy. No statement between line 57 and line 64 inspects the stream after writing, so the failure state is operated on by `targetFile.setCreationTime/...` (lines 60-62) and `return Result::ok();` (line 64), which reports successful extraction. Per the error/status-handling standard, attacker control of the triggering failure is not required; the security-relevant operation on the failure state is the success return, which silently accepts truncated/corrupt extraction.

CWE-400: `readEntireStreamAsString()` (line 44) allocates a String whose size equals the entire entry payload behind `in` (created at line 22 from attacker-controlled ZIP data). No shown statement bounds that payload size: the guards on this path are `entryPath.isEmpty()` (line 11), `isAChildOf` (line 16), `in == nullptr` (line 24), path/existence checks (lines 27-39), and `zei->entry.isSymbolicLink` (line 42) — none impose a length or size cap. A crafted symlink entry carrying a very large payload drives a proportional single heap allocation, enabling memory-exhaustion DoS.

assumptions: `zei->entry.filename`, `zei->entry.isSymbolicLink`, and the entry payload behind `in` are attacker-controlled ZIP metadata/data; the fragment itself imposes no size constraint on them (only the empty check at line 11 and the containment check at line 16).

`entries.getUnchecked` performs no bounds check (name-implied), and `File::createSymbolicLink`, `File::createDirectory`, `File::deleteFile`, and `hasSymbolicPart` behave per their standard names; their bodies are not shown.
`FollowSymlinks::no` (line 36) expresses the caller's intent not to write through symbolic links in the target tree.
limitations: Index OOB: `entries.getUnchecked (index)` (line 3) and `createStreamForEntry (index)` (line 22) consume the unconstrained `int` parameter, but the capacity of `entries` is not declared anywhere in the fragment, so a CWE-125 claim cannot be grounded.

Path traversal (`..`, absolute paths, backslash names): the containment guard `if (! targetFile.isAChildOf (targetDirectory))` (line 16) is the only boundary check, but its admitted set (whether it normalizes `..`/absolute components) is callee semantics not shown in the fragment; a bypass cannot be demonstrated, and a safe verdict cannot be derived from it either.

Directory entries: `return targetFile.createDirectory();` (lines 19-20) executes before the symlink-part gate at line 36, so the gate does not cover directory creates; likewise `exists()`/`deleteFile()` (lines 27-34) run before the gate, allowing an out-of-tree probe/delete before the failure return. Exploiting either requires an intermediate symlink, which the fragment can only create at line 47 in a prior unshown invocation — reachability within the shown code is not established.

Symlink target escape: `File::createSymbolicLink (targetFile, originalFilePath, true)` (line 47) accepts an unvalidated attacker-controlled target (absolute or `..`-containing); the security impact materializes only through later traversal or host application use, which is outside this fragment.
TOCTOU between `hasSymbolicPart` (line 36) and the write (line 57) would require concurrent external mutation of the target tree; no concurrency is shown.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable from the shown open_table() fragment. The suspicious spots (NULL alias reaching my_strcasecmp/my_error; memcmp length key_length at line 61; unguarded mdl_ticket assignment at line 194; debug assertions at 338/399) all fail Phase-3 confirmation: no in-fragment statement produces the NULL values, and the buffer capacities for the memcmp operands are not identifiable in the fragment. Protective statements are visible for db.str (line 42), share (line 218), and mdl_ticket on the non-HAS_MDL_LOCK path (lines 180-182).

assumptions: thd, table_list, and ot_ctx are internal-helper parameters supplied by a caller outside the fragment; the fragment itself never assigns NULL to table_list->alias.str, table_list->table_name.str, or table_list->mdl_request.ticket.

tdc_acquire_share(thd, table_list, gts_flags, &table) (line 216) is treated as an out-param API that sets *table on success, i.e., when it returns non-NULL share, `table` is defined before the read at 336.
err_lock (431) is reachable only after line 218's !share guard, so tdc_release_share(share) at 432 always receives a non-NULL share (all goto sites: 255, 261, 267, 271, 350, 373, 379).
thd->open_tables is a framework-managed NULL-terminated list, so the loop at line 58 terminates; no fragment code can create a cycle in that list.
get_table_def_key (line 48) returns a key and length that are consistent with each other by its name-implied contract; its body and buffer capacity are not shown.
limitations: NULL alias: `const char *alias= table_list->alias.str;` (line 6) reaches `my_strcasecmp(system_charset_info, table->alias.c_ptr(), alias)` (63) and `my_error` (110, 121, 123, 259, 425) with no shown NULL check and no in-fragment producer of NULL; a NULL would have to be caller-supplied, which is out of scope for a NULL-dereference finding.

memcmp (61): the length argument key_length (from line 48) is equal to table->s->table_cache_key.length under the guard at line 60, but the capacities of the `key` buffer and table_cache_key.str are not declared in the fragment, so any OOB-read boundary claim is unconfirmable.

mdl_ticket (194): on the MYSQL_OPEN_HAS_MDL_LOCK path the assignment `mdl_ticket= table_list->mdl_request.ticket;` is not NULL-checked and would be dereferenced at line 310 if share->tdc->flushed; producing NULL requires a caller contract violation, which is out of scope. First dereference of the out-of-domain table pointer from line 101: for an admitted `code >= CSIZE`, `codep` is at or beyond `&sp->dec_codetab[CSIZE]` (capacity from lines 106-107/114-115) and reading `codep->length` is an OOB heap read (CWE-125). The checks at 106-107 and 114-115 validate `free_entp`/`oldcodep`, not `codep`.

Secondary CWE-787: `occ` (line 6) has only the cast-fit check (line 20); no minimum check precedes the restart block, so `occ == 0` (and negative values) are admitted. With `sp->dec_restart != 0` produced by this fragment at line 154, `residue = codep->length - dec_restart >= 1` (line 30) passes `residue > occ` (line 31); `tp = op + occ` (line 42) equals `op`, so `*--tp` writes at `op - 1`, one byte before the `occ0 == 0`-byte region [op0, op0+occ0). The `while (occ > 0)` guard (line 74) is positioned after this sink and does not protect it.

Termination of the inner CODE_CLEAR loop (lines 79-87) and any parser-position stalls depend on NextCode's unshown output range and are not confirmable from the fragment.

verdict.summary: In glob()'s ~user tilde expansion, the terminating NUL is written one byte past an allocation of exactly end_name - dirname bytes (either the alloca_account or the malloc branch), producing a heap/stack one-byte out-of-bounds write reachable with an attacker-supplied pattern such as "~joe/x" under GLOB_TILDE (CWE-787).

evidence.reason: end_name - dirname (E) is both the allocation size (line 473 malloc / line 470 alloca_account) and the mempcpy length; the copy includes the '/' byte at dirname[E], and the NUL is stored at offset E, exactly one past the E-byte object whose capacity is declared at lines 469-473. Pattern "~joe/x" with GLOB_TILDE yields dirname="~joe/" (line 267), E=4; guards at lines 314, 316-318 (else), 448/464, 453-463, 481 all admit it (dirname[1]=='j', end_name non-NULL, unescape==NULL). mempcpy fills offsets 0-3 and '\0' lands at offset 4 == capacity: one-byte out-of-bounds NUL write, CWE-787.

Same missing +1 in the unescape branch: allocation is E = end_name - dirname (lines 469-473) with E <= dirlen-1, while p after the loop (lines 483-502) can reach index dirlen-1 or dirlen. Pattern "~x\\y/d/z" with GLOB_TILDE gives dirname="~x\\y/d" (dirlen=6, E=4): initial copy writes 1 byte, the loop emits 'y','/','d', so p = newp+4 and this NUL write lands at offset 4 of the 4-byte allocation, one byte past capacity — out-of-bounds NUL write, CWE-787.

assumptions: POSIX build: the #ifndef WINDOWS32 tilde-user block (lines 447-582) is the active path analyzed.
pattern is a NUL-terminated C string, as consumed by strlen/strchr/strrchr throughout the fragment.
GLOB_TILDE / GLOB_TILDE_CHECK are members of __GLOB_FLAGS: the fragment itself uses them as flag bits, so flags=GLOB_TILDE passes the line 16 check.
Both allocation branches (alloca_account, line 470, and malloc, line 473) reserve exactly end_name - dirname bytes; glob_use_alloca's body is not shown, but the OOB write holds on either path.
limitations: Possible use-after-free read of end_name after free(dirname) (lines 544-545 vs 562-564) is unconfirmable: it requires getpwnam/getpwnam_r to succeed on a constructed user_name that, per the shown copy logic, necessarily includes '/' and the whole dirname tail — an OS user-DB invariant not visible in the fragment.

Brace-expansion recursion depth (lines 146-148) is bounded by pattern length but could cause deep recursion/stack growth on very long patterns; no memory-unsafety consequence is demonstrated within the fragment.

GLOB_APPEND/GLOB_DOOFFS arithmetic with caller-supplied gl_offs (lines 183, 590, 732) could in principle involve size_t wraparound, but requires near-SIZE_MAX caller values the fragment never establishes; allocation-size checks (593, 741) then dominate.
Because glob_use_alloca's threshold is hidden, the corrupted memory region (heap vs. stack) and allocator layout are unknown; impact is a 1-byte NUL write either way.
The user_name string retains the '/' byte (same mis-sizing), which normally makes the subsequent getpwnam lookup fail; this does not prevent the out-of-bounds write, which occurs before the lookup.
The home-directory join at lines 415-431 is NUL-terminated (the last copied byte is dirname's own NUL), so the apparent missing-terminator concern is refuted.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable from the fragment alone. Every memory-safety candidate (prefix-chain descent of stackp below de_stack at lines 136/142/145 and the memcpy source reads at 156/169; the refill write to inbuf+insize at line 70; the outbuf writes at 99/156/169) requires buffer capacities that are not declared or derivable inside the shown code. On every path the fragment itself can construct, the derived indexes/sizes stay within the sizes the code itself maintains (e >= 0 at line 61; posbits realignments bounded by inbits; outpos+i clamped to OUTBUFSIZ at line 153). The strongest unconfirmed concern is the input-controlled, unbounded stack descent, which is recorded in limitations.

assumptions: OUTBUFSIZ equals outbuf's capacity: the shown code treats it as the flush bound (lines 151, 153, 159), but no declaration of outbuf is in the fragment.

read_buffer reads at most its size argument (INBUFSIZ) and returns -1 on error; input() is the standard two-byte bit reader using inbuf[posbits>>3] and advancing posbits by n_bits, per its call-site usage at line 93.
gzip_error (98, 132-134) and read_error (72) terminate; write_buf returns (129, 161, 185) are treated as intentionally ignored status values.
free_ent and table sizes are bounded by maxmaxcode = MAXCODE(maxbits) with maxbits <= BITS (lines 31, 33) on continuing paths.
limitations: Prefix-chain stack descent: lines 136, 142 and 145 can execute up to ~MAXCODE(maxbits) times for attacker-chosen codes (loop 140, bounded by free_ent at line 174), but de_stack's capacity is not declared and no named constant in the fragment is tied to it, so the OOB write below de_stack and the corresponding OOB source read in memcpy (156, 169) cannot be confirmed under the capacity-grounding rule.

Refill write (line 70) into inbuf+insize with size INBUFSIZ: the fragment's own transitions keep e = insize - (posbits>>3) >= 0 (line 61; realignments at 82-83/105-106 never exceed inbits, which is a multiple of 8*n_bits when rsize != 0, and rsize == 0 occurs only with insize < INBUF_EXTRA), so a negative insize is not producible from shown paths; it would require the unshown globals insize/inptr to satisfy insize < inptr.
outbuf bounds: writes at 99/156/169 are safe only under the unshown assumption that outbuf's capacity is OUTBUFSIZ (clamp at 153, flush at 159-164, guard at 151).

input() reads (line 93): the macro body is not shown; under the assumed two-byte read, the maximum source index is ((inbits - n_bits)>>3) + 1 <= insize - 1 on shown paths, so no overread is demonstrated, and inbuf's capacity is unidentifiable.

write_buf return values are discarded (lines 129, 161, 185): a failed write would silently drop output, but no security-relevant operation is shown running on that failure state (CWE-754 class unconfirmable).

gzip_error/read_error on malformed input (lines 72, 98, 132-134) are designed corrupt-input exits, not assertion violations of fragment-established invariants; input-triggered early termination of a decompressor is by-design behavior, not a confirmed CWE-617.
A valid LZW stream whose first code is CLEAR (256) is rejected at line 97 — a functional robustness issue with no demonstrated memory impact.
No NULL-dereference candidate exists: no shown call can produce NULL for inbuf/outbuf/de_stack/tab or the file descriptors.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read of the searched text buffer in bmexec_trans: the fragment places no bound on kwset->delta entries (unsigned char, residual 0..255) that are added to tp, so a single skip-loop pass can carry tp past text+size before the loop condition is re-tested, and the mid-pass tp[-1] dereferences (line 37, then line 69) read past the size-byte object; the memchr_kwset length argument at line 54 can likewise underflow to a huge size_t when tp overshoots the end.

evidence.reason: kwset->delta entries (unsigned char const*, residual range [0,255]; no shown bound) flow through `d = d1[U(tp[-1])]` into `tp += d` at lines 31-46. Witness: len=2, size=1000, where text is a 1000-byte object per the size parameter and `ep = text + size` (line 68); set d1[0xFF]=255 and text[1]=text[256]=text[511]=text[766]=0xFF. Line 28 admits tp=text+2 <= ep=text+978; after the advances at lines 31, 32, 35, 36 tp becomes text+1022, and line 37 evaluates tp[-1] = text[1021], 22 bytes past the last valid index 999 - CWE-125 out-of-bounds read. The `d != 0` guards at lines 33/38/43 admit 255, and no shown check between line 28 and line 37 re-bounds tp.

evidence.snippet: tp = memchr_kwset (tp, text + size - tp, kwset);
evidence.reason: Same root cause at a second sink. With len=2, size=25 (line 26 admits: 25 > 24) and deltas [2,2,2,2,2,2,2,2,2,7] (sum 25, nonzero at steps 2/5/8 so lines 33/38/43 admit), tp advances through in-bounds reads to text+27; line 51's guard (128 <= 25) is false so no big_advance; line 53 yields tp=text+26 > text+size. The length argument text+size-tp evaluates to -1 (ptrdiff) and converts to size_t ~SIZE_MAX, so memchr_kwset, a memchr-family call whose second parameter is a length, reads out of bounds from text+26 - CWE-125 via signed-to-unsigned length underflow at the call site.

assumptions: The (text, size) parameter pair defines a size-byte object: the fragment itself forms the end pointer `ep = text + size` (line 68) and passes size to memchr_kwset (line 15).
advance_heuristic = 16 * sizeof(long) (line 50) is at least 64, so the witness with delta sum 25 avoids the `goto big_advance` regardless of platform.
`d` assigned from an unsigned char element of d1 is always in [0,255] regardless of U's exact semantics, since d1's element type is `unsigned char const`.
int is assumed 32-bit for the arithmetic-overflow note in limitations.
limitations: The real kwset builder (kwsprep, unshown) clamps delta1 values to [1, len], which would make the skip loop safe; that invariant is outside the fragment and per the analysis rules cannot justify a safe verdict. The witnesses' delta magnitudes are drawn from the residual range [0,255] rather than from a value demonstrated by a shown statement, capping confidence at 0.65.

A zero entry in kwset->delta would stall `tp += d` and cause non-termination (CWE-835) in the skip loop (lines 28-64) and the tail loop (lines 70-77); this shares the same unconstrained-delta root cause, so it is not reported as a separate CWE.

Integer overflow of `12 * len` / `11 * len` (int) for len >= INT_MAX/12 is undefined behavior per C, but requires kwset->mind of roughly 1.8e8 with a matching buffer, so it is not demonstrated as an attacker path here.
The capacities of kwset->delta and kwset->target, and the bodies of bm_delta2_search and memchr_kwset, are not shown; no d1-index out-of-bounds or target-access claim is made.

verdict.summary: ReadStripMethod in ReadTIFFImage underflows the size_t counter rows_remaining when the file's RowsPerStrip tag is 0, so strips are never reloaded and p advances unchecked, causing a heap buffer over-read in ImportQuantumPixels (lines 778-781).

evidence.reason: File-controlled RowsPerStrip=0 (uint32, read line 556) is admitted by the only clamp (lines 565-566: 0 is not > image->rows); extent (line 727) is then 0 (or at most one scanline), so strip_pixels (lines 728-729) holds 0 bytes. At line 781 rows_remaining-- wraps from 0 to SIZE_MAX, so the reload guard at line 765 excludes every subsequent row, p (line 780) advances stride per row with no reload, and this call reads a full scanline from the 0-byte heap allocation on rows 0..image->rows-1 — heap buffer over-read (CWE-125), driven by the size_t underflow (CWE-191).

With rows_per_strip==0 admitted by lines 565-566, rows_remaining is 0 after line 771 and this decrement wraps the size_t to SIZE_MAX (CWE-191). The underflowed value is excluded by the reload guard at line 765, so no strip is ever re-read and the source pointer p keeps advancing (line 780) past the strip_pixels allocation whose capacity is fixed at line 727/728 — this is the root-cause wrap that converts a 0-row strip into the CWE-125 over-read.

assumptions: size_t/MagickSizeType are 64-bit on the LP64 target, so image->columns*image->rows cannot overflow and the generic RGBA path (lines 918-930) is exactly in-bounds.
rows_per_strip is declared uint32 (line 79) and image->rows=(size_t)height (line 258), so the clamp at lines 565-566 leaves residual range {0..image->rows} with 0 admitted.
MaxPixelChannels is 32 (line 4), bounding samples_per_pixel to {0..32} after the check at line 175.
limitations: The over-read requires libtiff to (a) return RowsPerStrip=0 from TIFFGetField (line 556), (b) return a non-(-1) result from TIFFReadEncodedStrip for a 0-row strip (lines 767-769, only -1 is rejected), and (c) AcquireQuantumMemory(0,...) (lines 728-729) to return non-NULL; none of these behaviors is visible in the fragment, so the exact excess depends on libtiff/allocation semantics.
Tiled images with TILEWIDTH/TILELENGTH of 0 would make the loops at lines 846/857 non-terminating (CWE-835), but delivery of 0 tile dimensions by libtiff is not shown in the fragment.

extra_samples (uint16, up to 65535, line 525) flows into pad (lines 628-643) and SetQuantumPad; an over-read inside ImportQuantumPixels would depend on its pad-skip semantics, which are not shown — not confirmed.

The size_t overflow of extent at line 727 (4*((depth+7)/8)*(spp+1)*TIFFStripSize) would require TIFFStripSize ~2^55; the path is normally pre-empted by the pixel-buffer allocation at line 598 or libtiff tmsize_t saturation — not confirmed.

Reads of whites/primary chromaticities (lines 334-353), sample_info (lines 536-549), and colormaps (lines 453-468) are consistent with the libtiff contracts implied by the shown field widths and allocations; no out-of-domain index is derived in the fragment.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability within the fragment. Every page access is bounded by the visible guards `while (curr < end)` with `end <= pptr + PAGE_CACHE_BITS/32` (lines 22-25, 41, 60-63, 90, 108), allocations are capped by `if (start >= size) goto out` and `len = min(size - start, len)` (lines 71-76) so `start + *max <= size`, `len >= 1` is established at line 11 before any `--len`, and all loops terminate (offset/len strictly advance). Remaining concerns -- unchecked read_mapping_page()/kmap() results, the function returning `size` on every path, and the unshown numeric value of PAGE_CACHE_BITS -- are unconfirmable from the fragment and listed in limitations.

assumptions: PAGE_CACHE_BITS names the bit capacity of one cached page and is a power of two; this is induced by the fragment itself, which uses `& (PAGE_CACHE_BITS - 1)` and `~(PAGE_CACHE_BITS - 1)` as modulo/mask (lines 19, 21, 25, 63) and `/ PAGE_CACHE_BITS` as page index (lines 17, 54, 57, 103, 104). Its numeric value is not defined in the fragment.

kmap(read_mapping_page(...)) maps one full page, so the word array `pptr..pptr + PAGE_CACHE_BITS/32 - 1` is the in-fragment-relevant capacity expression; the bound `end <= pptr + PAGE_CACHE_BITS/32` is visible at lines 23-25, 60-63 and 108.

Bit convention: `mask = (1U << 31) >> i` scanning with `start = offset + (curr - pptr) * 32 + i` (lines 31-33, 45-47, 70) is self-consistent only if bit 31 of a word is the lowest-numbered block; the analysis adopts this convention because it makes the fragment's own start/len accounting coherent.
sb, the alloc_file inode and *max are non-NULL (framework/caller pointers with no in-fragment NULL producer).
limitations: read_mapping_page() results (lines 17, 57, 104) are used by kmap()/set_page_dirty()/kunmap() without any IS_ERR/NULL check; a NULL/ERR_PTR page on I/O or allocation failure would be dereferenced (lines 18, 59, 106, 120). Not confirmed as a finding because the fragment shows no contract marking the result nullable and no in-fragment producer of the malformed pointer (framework-data rule).

The function returns `size` on every path, including the success fall-through from done: to out: (lines 119-129); success is distinguishable only through *max (line 123). Whether a caller misuses this return is not confirmable because no caller is shown.

Numeric values of PAGE_CACHE_BITS and the kmap'd page's byte capacity are not defined in the fragment, so any exact off-by-one claim against the page word array cannot be grounded numerically; bounds were verified symbolically via the visible `curr < end` and `end <= pptr + PAGE_CACHE_BITS/32` expressions.

For size/offset values near 0xFFFFFFFF, `offset += PAGE_CACHE_BITS` (lines 54, 103) can wrap u32 and re-scan a low page or produce a wrapped *max (line 123); this requires a ~2^32-block volume and is a logical/accounting concern, not a memory-safety violation, and the bitmap/file capacities involved are not shown.

`mask = 1 << 31;` (line 45) is a signed left shift into the sign bit (C UB); on kernel toolchains it yields 0x80000000 and the u32 scan behaves identically to the unsigned sites (lines 31, 112), so no malfunction is demonstrated from the shown types.
free_blocks (line 124) has an unshown type; subtraction underflow/accounting impact cannot be evaluated from the fragment.
Single-shot page-allocation failures (read_mapping_page) without a compounding attacker-controlled volume are treated as robustness concerns, not findings.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in bracketed_paste. The only security-relevant sink is the stack buffer buf[NUMBUFLEN + MB_MAXBYTES] (line 4) fed by loop input, but the STRNCMP prefix-match admission at line 39 (STRNCMP(buf, end, idx) == 0 implies idx <= STRLEN(end)) together with the end-length guard at lines 12-13 (non-NULL end implies STRLEN(end) < NUMBUFLEN) and the idx = 0 reset at line 87 keep every index below the declared capacity, so no value admitted by the guards reaches an out-of-capacity write. The PASTE_EX memmove (lines 56-57) is gated by ga_grow(gap, idx) == OK at line 54; all NULL-producing paths are handled at lines 12/24/39/54; no injection, crypto, file, auth, abort, or error-handling flaw is reachable.

assumptions: buf capacity is fixed by the declaration char_u buf[NUMBUFLEN + MB_MAXBYTES] at line 4; all writes must stay below this number of bytes.
find_termcode((char_u *)"PE") (line 6) returns a NUL-terminated string or NULL, consistent with the NULL checks at lines 12, 24, and 39 within the shown code.
mb_char2bytes(c, buf + idx) (line 35) writes at most MB_MAXBYTES bytes and returns the number of bytes written (name-implied contract; the fragment uses the return value to advance idx).

STRNCMP(buf, end, idx) (line 39) compares at most idx bytes and stops at an embedded NUL, per standard strncmp semantics; on this basis STRNCMP(...)==0 with buf NUL-terminated exactly at idx (line 38) implies idx <= STRLEN(end).
c == NUL is excluded before any buffer write (line 29), so buf[0..idx-1] contains no NUL bytes and line 38's terminator is exact.
ga_grow(gap, idx) == OK (line 54) is treated as the capacity check for the idx bytes copied at lines 56-58.
vgetc()/vpeekc() consume/probe the input typeahead, so each loop iteration makes forward progress on attacker-supplied input.
limitations: The macro values NUMBUFLEN and MB_MAXBYTES are not visible in the fragment; the symbolic proof (max write index <= NUMBUFLEN - 2 + MB_MAXBYTES, NUL at <= NUMBUFLEN - 2 + MB_MAXBYTES, both < NUMBUFLEN + MB_MAXBYTES) does not depend on their numeric values, but the exact safety margin does.

ga_itemsize and the body of ga_grow are not shown; the PASTE_EX memmove (lines 56-57) cannot be byte-level confirmed either safe or unsafe against gap->ga_maxlen, and no out-of-domain argument (negative or oversized size) is derived at the call site.

The bodies of put_on_cmdline, ins_char_bytes, AppendToRedobuffLit, ins_eol, and mb_ptr2char are not shown; no claim is made about their internal capacities, and the idx values passed are bounded and non-negative.
If mb_char2bytes could return 0 for an admitted c, idx would not advance but the loop would still consume a character; this is a robustness observation, not a memory-safety finding.
Silent dropping of paste data when stop_arrow() != OK (line 63) is a behavior quirk with no security-relevant operation running on the failure state.
The not-vulnerable verdict for the buf sink depends on the derived prefix-match invariant; if strncmp semantics differed from the standard contract assumed above, that bound would need re-derivation.

verdict.summary: The bitmap scan loop can run forever: `offset += PAGE_CACHE_BITS` (line 58) wraps a u32 to 0 when offset is the last page start, so the `if (offset >= size) break;` guard (line 59) never fires for large `size` values and the loop re-scans pages 0..2^32/PAGE_CACHE_BITS-1 indefinitely when the bitmap contains no zero bit. Inputs `size`/`offset` are unconstrained u32 entry-point parameters; a crafted image with an all-ones bitmap and `size` near 2^32 produces an unbounded loop (CWE-835) caused by integer wrap (CWE-190), i.e., a kernel hang/DoS.

evidence.reason: `offset` is an unconstrained u32 entry-point parameter (line 1, full domain [0, 2^32-1]); for offset = 2^32 - PAGE_CACHE_BITS the addition at line 58 wraps to 0, and line 59 then compares 0 >= size, which is false for the witness size = 0xFFFFFFFF, so the break is skipped and line 61 re-reads page 0. With a bitmap that never presents a zero bit (read_mapping_page data, no shown minimum), the outer loop (line 44) cycles pages 0..2^32/PAGE_CACHE_BITS-1 forever — every guard on the path (lines 11, 18, 63) admits the witness values. Primary mechanism is non-termination (CWE-835); the u32 wrap at line 58 is the independent root cause (CWE-190 secondary).

assumptions: PAGE_CACHE_BITS is the fragment's own page-bit unit; all end pointers remain within pptr + PAGE_CACHE_BITS/32 per the shown comparisons (lines 27-29, 45, 98, 120).
u32 arithmetic wraps modulo 2^32 (lines 29, 58, 111).
size and offset are filesystem-provided u32 parameters with no constraint in the shown code before use; *max must be >= 1 on the allocation path (lines 10-12).
The bitmap contents returned by read_mapping_page are unconstrained file data; the fragment never establishes the existence of a zero bit (lines 17, 32-56).
limitations: The physical byte capacity behind `pptr` is not declared in the fragment, so any out-of-bounds claim against the kmap'ed page is unconfirmable; all reads/writes obey curr < end in the fragment's own model (lines 45, 98).

The write-phase page advance (lines 109-120) lacks the offset >= size check present in the scan phase (line 59); traced behavior shows full-u32 writes stay within remaining real blocks via len accounting (lines 84, 100-107) and the extra page access at an exact page boundary is a value-preserving write-back with exact *max (line 135), so no OOB or corruption is confirmable without unshown file/mapping invariants.

If read_mapping_page fails at line 114 after earlier pages were dirtied (line 109), the function reports failure (start = size, line 115) with the bitmap partially allocated and free_blocks not updated; the failure trigger and downstream effect are not established in the shown code.
(size + 31) at lines 29/71 can wrap for size >= 2^32 - 31, collapsing `end`; this is subsumed by the confirmed non-termination finding and otherwise only shortens the scan.
kmap results (lines 22/67/118) and *max/sb pointers are not NULL-checked; NULL production is not shown in the fragment (caller/framework contract).
free_blocks -= *max (line 136) could underflow with a crafted counter, but no shown consumer of the corrupted counter exists in the fragment.
dprint format strings (lines 14/73/80/138) are fixed with %u args in scope — no format-string injection.
The found-bit guard start >= size (lines 79-82) correctly rejects out-of-range found positions; no violation traced on that path.

verdict.summary: bmexec_trans can read out of bounds: the skip loop advances tp by unconstrained delta entries (unsigned char d1[...], residual range [0,255], never capped against len in the shown code), allowing tp to pass text+size; the epilogue then unconditionally executes the sink d = d1[U(tp[-1])] (line 71) and mid-loop reads (e.g., lines 32, 35) can likewise access index >= size of the size-byte text buffer, yielding an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) on attacker-controlled text and pattern-derived skip tables.

evidence.reason: Unguarded initial epilogue read: capacity is the size-byte text region bounded by one-past pointer ep = text + size (line 70). tp is the product of the skip loop: with len=2, size=25 (guards at lines 9/11/13/26 admit: 2<=25 and 25>24), tp0=text+2<=ep=text+3 (line 28), ten delta entries of 13 each (unsigned char domain [0,255], residual range from line 3's `unsigned char const *d1`, never constrained relative to len in the shown code) advance tp to text+132 and pass the d!=0 guards (lines 33/38/43) and the 128<=130 heuristic (line 51, goto big_advance). The read at line 71 accesses index (size - 11*len) + S - 1 = 131 >= 25, i.e., 107 bytes past the 25-byte buffer: out-of-bounds read, CWE-125.

Earliest reaching overshoot read, same root cause: with len=2, size=25, a single admitted delta value d1=24 at line 31 advances tp from text+2 to text+26 with no intervening guard, and this line-32 read accesses text[25], i.e., index == size, 1 byte past the size-byte region bounded by text+size (line 70). The delta entries' residual range [0,255] (unsigned char, line 3) is the provenance; CWE-125 out-of-bounds read.

assumptions: U() is the standard kwset macro casting its argument to unsigned char, so d1 indices are in [0,255] and delta is byte-addressable (implied by its use as d1[U(...)]).
text is treated as a size-byte readable buffer with one-past end text+size, established by lines 15, 21, 28, 54, and 70.

verdict.summary: In S_study_chunk, the CURLY fixed-substring path derives the SvGROW/repeatcpy capacity as (mincount * l) + 1 where l is the BYTE length of the accumulated literal (line 1199) while the 'Regexp out of space' guard (line 1032) bounds mincount only against minnext, the CHARACTER length (line 756). On an ILP32 build, a bounded quantifier over a multi-byte UTF-8 literal (e.g. /€{1431655766}/) wraps the size so SvGROW allocates a few bytes and repeatcpy writes ~4 GiB, a heap buffer overflow.

evidence.reason: mincount (SSize_t, from ARG1 at line 937) is admitted up to 2^31-2 by the guard at line 1032, whose bound uses minnext (character length, after the char conversion at line 756) while l at line 1199 is the byte length of the literal (e.g., l=3 for one 3-byte UTF-8 char). On a 32-bit STRLEN build, (mincount*l)+1 wraps (1431655766*3+1 == 3), so SvGROW allocates 3 bytes and repeatcpy(dest=SvPVX+3, len=3, count=mincount-1) writes 3*(mincount-1)=4294967295 bytes past the 3-byte allocation at line 1217-1219: heap buffer overflow (CWE-787) whose root cause is the integer wrap in the size (CWE-190), reachable because the guard at line 1032 is in the character domain and never constrains the byte product.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable from the shown fragment. Every buffer sink (pixel buffer line 600/604, strip buffer 729-734, tile buffer 824-830, generic RGBA buffer 920-926) is sized consistently with its writer under the shown guards: number_pixels >= scanline_size (599), spp <= 32 (177), rows_per_strip <= height (567-568), and extent >= 8*TIFFStripSize / >= rows*TIFFTileRowSize. Confidence is capped below 0.8 because the safe verdict rests on thorough per-sink consistency analysis rather than a single decisive protective statement.
